subsubtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OF PULP AND PAPER MILLS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter urgent to the entire newspaper industry of Canada. Whereas this industry receives less than 7 per cent of Canada's newsprint production, the rest being exported, and whereas a number of pulp and paper mills are threatened with strikes, which will severely reduce newsprint supplies, and in view of the proposed adversiting tax changes for newspapers instigated by the government, which will impose severe hardships on the industry, and which have been described by
Patrick O'Callighan as "Unprecedented attempts to intrude into the traditional freedom of the press", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That this House request the merciless Minister of Finance to cease his Big Mac attack on the newspaper industry, that the government encourage the mills to avoid any strikes, and encourage these mills to allocate a further 2 per cent of their production to Canada, in order that Canadians may continue to read such earth-shaking events as the Prime Minister's infamous sheik-yer-bootie two-step hustle, or the NDP Leader's enjoyment of Cuban cigars, plus the profound political insight provided daily by columnists such as Allan Fotheringham.

subsubtopic: RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE BETWEEN BARRIE AND TORONTO- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43. There is an omission which is inconveniencing thousands of residents along the west shore of Lake Simcoe who regularly commute from Barrie to Toronto. Present service is inadequate, and surveys taken indicate there is both commuter demand and potential. The president of VIA Rail has stated that provinces should contract with VIA Rail to "run trains where local interests feel they should go". Residents of Simcoe South are caught between conflicting jurisdictions, VIA Rail and GO, neither of which presently satisfy popular demand. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Minister of Transport use his good offices with VIA Rail and GO (Ontario) to expedite a contract or a swap of passenger runs which will result in improved commuter service and passenger profits for the rail carrier.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to propose a motion which I am sure will receive the unanimous consent of the House. Since the U.S. based National States Rights Party, which describes itself as "by far the largest white racist party in America", has established its mailing address at one of Canada's post offices in Toronto's east end and has distributed copies of its publication "The Thunderbolt" to many households in that area, and since on Sunday last the Ku Klux Klan engaged in a public cross burning in British Columbia, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper):
That this House condemn in the strongest terms the race hatred and intimidation used by organizations such as the National States Rights Party and the Ku Klux Klan, and since prohibitory orders have been issued by the post office against the National States Rights Party and "The Thunderbolt" magazine, that the Postmaster General investigate the possible use of other post offices by this organization.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Ever since the announcement of the Petro-Canada takeover of Petrofina, we on this side have been very concerned about the obvious indications of insider trading leading up to the acquisition of the company by Petro-Canada. I am sure the Prime Minister is aware of the article which appeared this morning in The
Oral Questions
Toronto Sun which outlined substantial profits that were made in the period leading up to the takeover. It makes some very serious allegations as to the involvement of cabinet ministers and of a senator. What steps has the Prime Minister taken to assure himself that these allegations are not true? Can he assure the House that no cabinet minister made any material profit as a result of insider trading in these shares?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have not had the time nor, I must say, the inclination to read the Sun article.
Oh, oh!

I remember that this kind of innuendo was brought up in the House a few weeks ago by members opposite, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs undertook to refer the matter to the Ontario Securities Commission, which he did. We will hear from the Ontario Securities Commission, which is looking into this matter as it should, and I am sure the securities commission will be able to give the hon. member assurance that no cabinet minister was involved.
You are sure of that?
That is very casual.

Madam Speaker, I am very, very surprised at the statement by the Prime Minister that he does not have the inclination to look into this article, which has some very serious allegations contained in it.
I never read garbage.
Start looking.

The article further alleges that a company connected with Maurice Strong was also involved in very substantial profits arising out of the transaction. Since Mr. Strong was in a position of trust as a principal participant in the negotiations leading up to the takeover, has the Prime Minister had any discussions with Mr. Strong to assure himself that Mr. Strong is not involved with Sofigen, the company alleged to be involved in these profits.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as to the preamble to the question, 1 am surprised that the hon. member is surprised. I think it is well-known that I do not read the newspapers very much, but I particularly do not read those that publish garbage.
Hear, hear!
As to the question itself, no, I have not spoken to Maurice Strong about it.

You don't care about it.

June 2, 1981
Oral Questions
Never garbage. That is what you are reading all the time.

Madam Speaker, I am sure the Prime Minister is going to realize very soon that this is a matter of great concern to Canadians at large, and they do not regard this as garbage, rather they regard it as a very serious matter.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister referred a minute ago to the steps taken by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who agreed under some pressure from us about two months ago to undertake an investigation.
Would the Prime Minister outline the status of the investigation to this House? In addition, would he advise the House whether this investigation, as it is presently constituted, will address the allegations which are outlined in The Toronto Sun article?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is obvious that this investigation is continuing. It is now being carried out by officials of my department in the Bureau of Corporate Affairs, by the Ontario Securities Commission and by the Quebec Securities Commission. It is obvious that the allegations published today in a Toronto newspaper will indeed be followed up and studied by the people who are now making that investigation.
Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Prime Minister. Even if the Prime Minister does not read garbage, fortunately or unfortunately a lot of people in this country do read garbage.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

He should not try to slough off an important matter such as this, which I suggest to the Prime Minister casts a cloud, certainly over all cabinet ministers if not all members of this House. May I just say, for the benefit of the Prime Minister, that the allegation is that there were purchases of Petrofina stock made just prior to the takeover by PetroCan. This involves a senator and his wife, two unnamed cabinet ministers, and a named cabinet minister, through an investment company, and some of these through nominee accounts.
These are important allegations that should not and cannot be sloughed off by the Prime Minister. If for nothing other than his own peace of mind, I would have imagined he would have inquired into the matter and would have reported here today. Will the Prime Minister please tell us what investigations he has made and what are the results of those investigations into alleged improprieties on the part of members of his cabinet?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take note of the admission by the hon. member that some people do read garbage, namely, the people on the other side of the House. I can say that that is their problem. In so far as cabinet ministers are concerned, my information is that one was named, the member from Hamilton. I inquired of him, and he has already protested to the paper, asking for an apology because there is absolutely no foundation in fact in the allegations made against that minister. I hope the newspaper will make a very strong apology.
In the case of other allegations of unnamed people, I do not know. If there are some people who made money in a way they should not have, I trust the Ontario Securities Commission will determine that. As the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs told the House, he is also making an investigation. Between the two of them, one a federal investigation and the other an investigation by the Ontario Securities Commission, we will find out if there are some guilty people. If so, I hope their names will be made public and that they will be taken to trial. However, I do not know of any. Until the Ontario Securities Commission in particular has finished its inquiry, I think it is a bit premature to publish the names of "guilty persons".

There are a couple of corrections implicit in that. At least one cabinet minister reads garbage. The second correction involves the investigation by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who has been quoted as indicating that in all likelihood the federal investigation, apart from the Ontario Securities Commission investigation, will not be made public. I would like the Prime Minister to expand on this and indicate to us why in any event before it is even completed there is an indication that it may not be made public. Why can we not have an understanding and commitment from the Prime Minister now, regardless of which names are mentioned, that that report will be made public. We have every right to know.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member says that we now have the admission of one cabinet minister that he reads garbage. The important admission is the one by the hon. member in his two questions that in fact it is garbage he has been reading. That is the main point. In so far as the Ontario Securities Commission is concerned, I have no control over it. I trust that Premier Bill

Davis, a good Conservative, will ensure that any truth that should come to light will come to light.

subsubtopic: ADVICE TENDERED TO MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to turn to some other garbage, the government's economic policy. My question is to the minister whose genius speaks for itself, the Minister of Finance. Is the minister aware that Governor Bouey told the Senate committee on national finance, and I quote from the transcript:
I think the economy is not all that far off from being as close to potential as it should be.
However, the Economic Council of Canada has stated in its annual report:
-this country is not making full use of its available human resources and of its plant, machinery and equipment.
I would ask the minister whose advice is he currently following; is he following the advice of Governor Bouey when he says that Canada is working at full potential, or is he following the advice of the Economic Council of Canada which says that Canada is not working at its full potential?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ADVICE TENDERED TO MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in certain cases I follow the advice of neither. I want to make it clear to the hon. member that in so far as the administration and thrust of monetary policy are concerned, and I have stated so frequently, I obviously support the Bank of Canada, but it is not my intention to comment and adjudicate upon every statement made either by the Governor of the Bank or the chairman of the Economic Council before any committee to which they are summoned. I am not going to get into that business, and it is not my responsibility to vet their opinions.

subtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON GROWTH AND PRODUCTIVITY
EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON GROWTH AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is the minister's responsibility to make up his mind as to whether or not he thinks the economy is at its full potential, and what policy he intends to carry out to see that that takes place. That is what we are waiting to hear from the minister. I would like to ask the minister this supplementary question before he gets totally agitated. When the chairman of the Economic Council tells the finance committee, as he did on Friday, that the interest rate policy of the government is above what is sensible from the point of view of achieving this general objective of full capacity, full potential and the full use of our economy, is the minister not concerned that the effect of high interest rates at the present time is to discourage real growth and real productivity in the economy, particularly
Oral Questions
when all the evidence suggests that unless we have an economy working at capacity we are not going to achieve the growth and productivity he says he wants?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON GROWTH AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, though 1 heard about the testimony given by the chairman of the Economic Council, based upon news reports, I have not been able to receive a transcript. I have attempted to get a transcript. 1 have learned that oftentimes the transcript of the actual evidence carries a somewhat different interpretation than abbreviated newspaper accounts. I have not seen the testimony of the chairman of the Economic Council.
The hon. member talks about the necessity of growth and what our policy is in that regard. He ought to know that in the fourth quarter of last year the annual rate of growth in the economy was 8 per cent, and in the first quarter of this year it was 3 per cent to 6 per cent, a rate of growth which, in my opinion, is not compatible with the long-term necessity of reducing inflationary expectations in this country. If he believes in fighting inflation, then he ought to put that particular fact into his calculations.

subtopic: RELATIVITY OF TAXES ON BANKS AND ON INDIVIDUALS
RELATIVITY OF TAXES ON BANKS AND ON INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the calculations which are given to us by the Economic Council, and the calculations given to us on what is really going on in the economy from the point of view of idleness in the economy, idle hands and idle machinery and lost hopes, are published and there for all to see, and the minister can put them into his calculations if he wants.
The final question I have for the minister has to do with the proposals he has been making on a so-called tax-based incomes policy. When the industrial wage since 1970 has gone up 150 per cent, whereas direct taxes on persons have gone up 300 per cent, and when bank profits have gone up 210 per cent, but their taxes paid to the Canadian public have gone up 14 per cent, and when you put those figures into your calculations, which I hope you will take the trouble to do, how can you go around the country talking about punishing workers-

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister has said an inquiry is being undertaken. We know that when inquiries are into oil companies, the results are published immediately. speechtext: Madam Speaker, as to the allegation of hon. members opposite, I am reminded that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicated to the House that cabinet ministers heard about the Petrofina deal at 5 p.m. on Thursday, January 29, when the market was closed. I do not just go around suspecting people of being dishonest. I know that is a different attitude toward life

than that of the Leader of the Opposition, but that is my attitude.

subtopic: ALICE ARM, B.C.-CLOSING OF AMAX MINE
ALICE ARM, B.C.-CLOSING OF AMAX MINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Late last week the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans requested that the Amax operation at Alice Arm be closed, and that was done. The reason the minister stated in his telex to the company last week for his request for closure has now been confirmed to be true; in fact the tailings at about five parts per million are above the 100 metre level.
Could the minister tell this House what steps or modifications he has requested of the company so that the tailings will not resurface? Is it his position today that that mine can reopen without modification?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: ALICE ARM, B.C.-CLOSING OF AMAX MINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just returned after some days of absence. I saw the information alluded to by the hon. member.
Yes, the company did comply with the request I made of it. We are checking into the material which seems to have surfaced above the level which was permitted by the regulations. I am meeting some of my officials to discuss this very question at three o'clock, and I hope to answer the hon. member's question more fully tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, it is costing the company an estimated $350,000 a day to be closed down, while the minister travels in other areas of the country. The minister had a study done which demonstrates that the tailings ponds on land could be undertaken safely and economically for a cost of $26 million, or $ 1 million per year of mine operation, which is only a 2 per cent difference in return on investment.
Since four out of five of the government's own scientists recommended against marine dumping, which has now been proven to pollute the environment above the one hundred metre level, will the minister now either recommend to the company that they use on-land tailings ponds, or support the idea of a full public inquiry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my absence had nothing to do with the delay. The fact is, and we said so in the telegram, that delay was caused pending examination of the material by scientists. Surely the hon. member, who has been doing his best to have the whole operation closed down, cannot today have the comfort of saying he is trying to stop the company from losing money because we are asking that precautions be taken. He had better make up his mind what he wants to do.
The fact is, Madam Speaker, that we are checking into this problem, and in this situation we will take a responsible position and do what is necessary. I am not going to prejudge the scientists' recommendations.

June 2, 1981
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, the minister sort of callously brushes aside the $350,000 a day costs that are accruing to the company, but it is abundantly clear to this House that four out of five scientists recommended against it. Has the minister recommended to the company any modifications in the dumping which has proven to be polluting contrary to the special order in council, and is it his position that the mine can reopen today?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. In this case, since the fishing has not taken place, it is difficult for the board to make a judgment, but I will ask them to examine this and see if there is in fact any room under the legislation as it exists for them to make recommendations to the government.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence and relates to the alarming rate of resignations and early retirement of long service senior Armed Forces personnel, a rate abnormally higher than the normal rate of attrition. I ask the minister is he aware that this phenomenon is as a result of low morale, unification, lack of separate identity, and because our forces are underequipped, undermanned and overextended? I also ask whether he is taking steps to stem this exodus, by monitoring morale and other problems created by unification, as I did through this direct mailer I hold in my hand, to my constituents in the Armed Forces, and is he aware that Armed Forces
personnel were ordered by their superior officers not to reply to me through this questionnaire?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would rather answer in French the question just put to me by the hon. member concerning the allegedly very low morale of our Armed Forces, and the early retirement of certain of our generals and senior officers. Such retirements are normally due to the fact that our senior officers, because of their outstanding competence and very thorough training in the Armed Forces, want to launch a new career in private enterprise or in the public service, anxious as they are to serve their country in a different capacity.
Madam Speaker, I have no indication that morale in the Armed Forces is at its lowest; on the contrary, since this government has re-equipped the Armed Forces with the best equipment possible and considering that their pay scale has recently been raised to a satisfactory level, I think that the morale of the Armed Forces is better than it has ever been.

Madam Speaker, in my view the minister's reply indicates his office has little or no understanding of this serious problem. Will the minister explain why 86 per cent of the respondents to the questionnaire said that morale was low, 84 per cent favoured separate identities and uniforms, and 74 per cent said unification was not working and was not effective?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Minister of National Defence

Madam Speaker, 1 think one can indeed expect a reaction to a questionnaire which begins with a sentence like this, and I quote:
I am very proud of the Canadian Armed Forces personnel, but I believe their morale is very low, that they are underequipped and that our Armed Forces are over-extended.
In my opinion, when a questionnaire begins on such a negative note, I cannot understand how people can answer in an unbiased mood.

subsubtopic: MECHANICAL DEFECTS IN AUTOMOBILES-ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Just over a year ago, as reported at page 1532 of Hansard, I asked the minister about rabbits-Volkswagen Rabbits, that is. The
Oral Questions
question concerned a serious and recurring compound failure of the braking system in Volkswagen Rabbits. At that time the minister undertook to investigate the matter and to bring about remedial action through representations to Volkswagen.
The minister should be aware that in December of this year an internal report produced evidence that there have been over one hundred documented brake failures in Volkswagen Rabbits in Canada, over 1,000 in the United States, and that, in fact, these brake failures are far in excess of the rate of failures in similar cars. For example, in the case of all similar class vehicles there was only one other failure in all other types of vehicles.
Since 12 months have passed since I First raised this question, can the minister tell the House why he has chosen to do nothing to ensure the absolute safety of owners of Volkswagen Rabbit cars? Is it true that the minister has instructed his officials to back off Volkswagen, to avoid embarrassment or potential costly recalls to them?

subsubtopic: MECHANICAL DEFECTS IN AUTOMOBILES-ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the last allegation is certainly false. I would not do that, for sure.
Recently there was a communique from my department with regard to the number of automobiles recalled in the last year. At the time I was assured that none were pending. The hon. member has again raised the question of the Volkswagen Rabbit, which I will look into again, but I have no reason to believe there were any difficulties with respect to that car.

Madam Speaker, I personally received a large number of documented complaints with respect to accidents involving Volkswagen Rabbits, with brake failure as the principal cause. Bearing in mind that Volkswagen has refused to meet the repair costs to owners resulting from these failures, and given the fact that there have been many accidents and that there could well be more accidents and possible deaths, and in order to prevent a recurrence of further such accidents in the future, is the minister prepared to implement the defect notification procedures of the Motor Vehicle Safety Act and to demand compensation from Volkswagen? I might add that Volkswagen has chosen to compensate owners who take Volkswagen Canada to small debts court, but otherwise it refuses to meet the costs of repair.

Madam Speaker, I now recall very clearly that, indeed, action was taken with regard to this matter. Volkswagen issued instructions to people as to the proper use of the car.
On the subject of recall in general, I am sure the hon. member would like to know that 50 per cent of people who are entitled to repairs free of charge do not avail themselves of that right.

June 2, 1981
Oral Questions THE ECONOMY

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance. In a recent speech the Premier of Alberta implied that responsibility for high interest rates can be attributed to the failure to reach an energy agreement with the federal government. Can the minister confirm or deny this theory?

Madam Speaker, obviously one could speculate indefinitely about the causes of higher interest rates. However, I would indicate that it is the very nature of our economic system which explains that increases in interest rates are due, first and foremost, to a greater demand for money and for credit, and to all sorts of other developments occurring on the money markets.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY TO DETERMINE WHETHER INDUSTRY IS IN PUBLIC INTEREST
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and is a different one from the others on this topic in which he was engaged earlier. A few days ago the Prime Minister defended Canada's participation in the international uranium cartel as being in the public interest, to paraphrase him somewhat. Yesterday, in a leaked document from an internal study conducted by EMR, various options to rescue and expand the atomic energy industry, which is currently suffering from terminal economics, were discussed.
Does the government have any hard evidence to prove that expansion of the nuclear industry, considering all the risks involved, is, indeed, in the so-called public interest? Will the Prime Minister assure the House that before any more nuclear reactors are imposed on the people of Canada, or any more money-losing exports are made to foreign countries, a detailed and comprehensive study will be undertaken to prove that our nuclear industry is, indeed, in the Canadian public interest?

Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources): Madam Speaker, at present there are no plans to build new reactors in Canada. I think it will be several months, even years before decisions are made with respect to that. As far as potential exports are concerned, the hon. member is no doubt aware of the fact that we are now negotiating with various countries, namely, Korea and Roumania, for the sale of additional reactors. This would ensure the viability of our nuclear industry and would also allow us to create new jobs which would certainly benefit all Canadians.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY TO DETERMINE WHETHER INDUSTRY IS IN PUBLIC INTEREST
speechtext: Madam Speaker, Dr. Strangelove would have been enthusiastic about a reply of that nature.

Among the options offered by the EMR study to rescue the nuclear industry are the following: lowering Canada's international safeguard provisions, the milk-cow policy of building border stations to export power to the United States, and increasing federal subsidies in order to entice more provinces to build yet more nuclear reactors. Has the minister considered a no expansion policy for the atomic industry and the redirection of the hundreds of millions of dollars we are spending on this industry annually, shifting these funds into decommissioning and into waste disposal studies for the existing industry, as well as increasing encouragement incentives for conservation and a switch to alternative energy sources and technology?

Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague probably received a watered down version of the study conducted by my officials because that was one of the options mentioned. The study was conducted by a departmental official, but, as I said, it is only a draft. We will be consulting with the industry and with those concerned, including groups opposed to nuclear power. Such consultations will take place this week and the next. Afterwards, the study will be reviewed, examined and improved and hopefully we will at some time in the future be able to make public a study which will be the final result of our consultations. Until then, however, it remains a working paper enumerating various options, of which the hon. member only gave a partial list. So I would suggest that he perhaps try to get a copy under the table somewhere.

MR. STEWART-DISTRIBUTION OF QUESTIONNAIRE TO ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on what I consider something that has impeded my ability to function properly as a member of this House. On October 11, 1974, at page 343 of Hansard, the then minister of national defence, the Hon. James Richardson, stated as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to confirm in unqualified terms that any member of the Armed Forces is able to write to a member of Parliament on any subject with exactly the same freedom as any other citizen of Canada.
Apparently this is not the case in 1981. In March of this year, while carrying out my duties as member of Parliament for Simcoe South, I distributed a questionnaire in my riding and to members of the Armed Forces at Base Borden concerning a very public document, the Fyffe report. This report was brought down at the request of the then minister of national defence, my colleague the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. June 2, 1981

McKinnon). I have since collaborated on the same type of questionnaire with the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), who has experienced the same result.
It has been brought to my attention, Madam Speaker, that Armed Forces personnel have been ordered not to reply to this questionnaire. Despite this edict, I received almost 200 written replies, most of them signed, and dozens of telephone calls. One respondent wrote as follows:
Service personnel are instructed not to answer this questionnaire.
A second stated as follows:
My husband received your questionnaire at his office but was strongly instructed through a letter ... not to answer the form.

I have a tendency to do that because when members insist on the presence of the minister in order to bring up their question of privilege, I have had the experience that the purpose in most cases is to turn the matter into a debate.
I have a precedent here from which I can quote. I think it will allow hon. members to agree with me that this does not constitute a prima facie case of privilege. It is a case on which Speaker Jerome ruled on February 20, 1975 and had to do with Air Canada and a labour dispute, at which time the corporation had asked its members not to answer a questionnaire. So the situation is quite similar. The then Speaker ruled that he could not extend the definition of a question of privilege to that particular circumstance, and he said as follows:
The consequences of extending that definition of privilege to innumerable areas outside this chamber into which the work of an MP might carry him, and particularly to the great number of grievances he might encounter in the course of that work, would run contrary to the basic concept of privilege.
Speaker Jerome went on to say concerning the definition of privilege that he could not find that there had been an impediment to the member of Parliament in his work because certain members had not been allowed to answer a questionnaire.
I would say that this has to do with the administration and the rules within the Armed Forces. If hon. members feel that those rules are not helpful to them in the carrying out of their work, they should file a grievance in the appropriate place, that is to say, with the minister. This matter should be discussed with the minister either in the House or elsewhere.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) I think was very close to admitting that it might not be a question of privilege. My judgment now is that it is not a question of privilege.
If the hon. member wants the minister to explain the rules and procedures within the Armed Forces, then I think he will recognize that can be done in the House on other occasions, that it is debate but does not constitute a prima facie case of privilege.

For what reason does the government's fiscal year run from April 1 to March 31, rather than from January 1 to December 31?

The
fiscal years are chosen for reasons of administrative convenience. The federal government's fiscal year end was changed from June 30 to March 31 in 1906 after Parliament began sitting for a longer period each year. This change, to March 31, made it possible to prepare the public accounts for tabling while the House was still in session. There have been no convincing reasons put forward since that date to warrant changing the fiscal year end to another date. It is not uncommon for the fiscal year of governments to differ from the calendar year. All provincial governments in Canada, and many governments of other industrialized countries, have chosen fiscal years which differ from the calendar year.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have left in the time allotted to me, I want to bring to the attention of the House the fact that I take exception to the statement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) that he is trying to keep down the cost of oil and gas in Canada and that Canadians are enjoying a cheaper price than people in other parts of the world. Naturally they are to a degree because the province of Alberta is prepared to grant that concession. Nevertheless, there are two or three points that have to be made.
Canadians must be aware of the cost of this subsidy, this one-price system across Canada. The federal government is paying out $3.6 billion each year for this subsidy so that there will be this one price across Canada. This works out to approximately $150 per person, or $600 per family. Normally a family is referred to as four persons, which seems reasonable.
With each family paying $600 a year to provide that subsidy, plus additional taxes, over a four-year period that works out to approximately $4,500. It is one of those instances where the minister has not been honest with the Canadian people. When you consider that the people are taxed three and a half cents a gallon for Petrofina, plus the oil subsidy, it will cost them about $4,500 over four years. The Canadian people should be aware of that.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act to provide for a revenue tax with respect to petroleum and gas. I rise to express my concern over the provisions in this bill which will raise the excise tax on beer and ale products far ahead of the relative tax increases on hard liquor.
I understand this tax will increase 29 per cent for beer, 155 per cent for wine and 6 per cent for hard liquor. This government's economic policies and tax policies are enough to drive anyone to drink. However, if the Canadian public is going to turn to drinking, the situation should be improved so that there will be more of a concession for soft liquor rather than hard liquor. As a result of the extra cost of the excise tax, the transportation of beer and so on, the average worker will be forced to change his style of drinking from beer to hard liquor.
As we know, the brewery industry creates a lot of employment. I would like to relate the figures for British Columbia. The B.C. beer industry employs directly 1,160 people, the B.C. winery employs 309 and the B.C. distillers 389 people. It is obvious that the beer industry employs almost twice as many people, to say nothing of those employed by related industries, including return of bottles and other activities connected with serving beer.
Everyone knows that beer is the drink of the working people. The working people expect to be able to relate more to soft liquors than hard liquors. It seems to me that only the Canadian government would adopt a policy changing the emphasis from soft liquor to hard liquor, a policy which encourages people to use hard liquor rather than soft liquor. The government appears to be doing this by placing a heavy tax burden on beer drinkers in Canada and a lesser tax burden on those who drink hard liquor. I think this is wrong, and I am sure we will increase social problems if we allow this kind of taxation to take place. People will turn to the use of hard liquor and we will see an increase in related problems, including drinking and driving and more alcoholism.
I should like to make a few comments based on a study which has already been carried out. It indicates that we have already seen the impact of this change in consumer drinking habits. Since the change was announced last April, hard liquor sales have increased by nearly 5 per cent while beer sales have dropped off 3.6 per cent and wine sales have decreased at least 2 per cent. I suggest this pattern will have an effect on the health of Canadians and increase traffic dangers because of an increase in alcoholism.

June 2, 1981

It is important to note that beer is the traditional drink of the average working Canadian. We cannot overemphasize that fact. I would urge the government to reconsider this bill before us because it will result in heavier taxation of the working people of Canada, which in turn will change their drinking habits.
The impact of this measure on the agricultural sector will also be severe. Some 63 per cent of agricultural products used by the liquor industry in Canada is used by the brewery industry. If this trend in decreasing beer sales continues, there will be a very severe impact on the producers of hops who supply the breweries. We can ill afford to see this decrease in our agricultural base.
We should be encouraging people to produce more agricultural products and to increase our agricultural base, particularly those who supply our brewery industry which uses such a significant amount of agricultural produce. Last year brewery purchases of agricultural products amounted to almost $100 million.
How much harder can we hit the working people? We are increasing costs to the brewery industry not only by increasing taxes, but also through the increase in the cost of energy and the cost of transporting their products in this province and throughout Canada.
Let me also comment on the indexation formula in this bill. It is the government's intention to increase indexation automatically without having to come back for parliamentary approval. That is not good enough. We do not want to see any increase in taxes without parliamentary approval. The fact that this government intends to index taxation on an ongoing, automatic basis without having to come back to Parliament for consideration and debate, and without allowing representatives of the industry to point out the difficulties such an increase will have, is something I do not think any member of Parliament should allow to happen.
It is difficult enough to try to make changes when we are allowed to consider and debate a taxation measure, but to allow indexing of taxation to take place automatically, with its consequential impact on the brewery industry, or on any other industry, without bringing a bill before Parliament for debate is unacceptable. We do not agree with that aspect of this measure.
The second part of our amendment would eliminate all taxes on liquor as proposed in this bill. We are saying the government should go back to the drawing board and come up with a tax system which will discourage increased use of hard liquor and encourage growth of the Canadian brewery industry. If it is the intention of people to drink alcoholic products, we would like to see them drink soft liquors. Our taxation system should be directed to making it easier for working people to drink soft liquors rather than hard liquors, which appears now to be the trend. We feel this is right because of the effect to use of hard liquor can have on the individual and because of the increase in social problems within the family, within the community and throughout Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add some comments to the debate on this bill. In particular, I want to speak to the amendments which deal with the definition of "manufacturing". I want to demonstrate to members what happens when definitions are loose and imprecise, and when bureaucrats decide to play games with definitions such as that of manufacturing.
In 1977 a Toronto-based entrepreneur decided to become a manufacturer of bicycles. The company involved was long established in the bicycle trade. The management and senior staff could be classed as experts on bicycles. The company was started by Harry D. Shields and it bore his name as a limited liability private corporation. Mr. Shields, Sr. had retired from active participation in the business and the company was being managed and operated by his son Lome Shields, who had grown up in the business, so to speak. He would be considered an expert in the Canadian market and in the sourcing of bicycles and components from suppliers anywhere in the world.
At the time of the events I am going to relate the bicycle manufacturing industry in Canada was in serious condition. The largest manufacturer, CCM, had posted several years of losses and the owners believed the company would not survive if some tariff protection was not put in place. After a hearing before the Anti-dumping Tribunal a tariff was placed against bicycles manufactured in South Korea and Taiwan.
Mr. Shields' knowledge of the Canadian market alerted him to the possibility that the Anti-dumping Tribunal would bring down a decision against imported bicycles from Taiwan and South Korea. He made a basic decision, sir, to become a manufacturer of bicycles. He set about organizing his venture. He leased a plant, acquired machinery and began assembling a staff to get production off the ground.
In manufacturing, if you are large enough you can design a product, build a prototype, test it, source components, place orders to subcontractors for some of those components and begin to manufacture. That is the textbook approach.
In Lome Shields' case he knew the market because he had been in it for years. He knew he could sell all the bicycles he could make, so his task was to get hold of that market first and then search around for Canadian components after he had a good hold on the market. Like most manufacturers, his market sense told him it would be more profitable if he could ship from the end of his production line to his customers rather than build to inventory. He had pre-sold a year's production on this basis.
With all the excitement and pressure to get his operation off the ground, Mr. Shields had not reckoned with the bureaucracy of the Department of National Revenue. There has been an ongoing debate between Revenue Canada and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce regarding the difference between manufacturing, assembling, processing and producing. If we go through the numerous statutes, we will find a

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
variety of definitions which are usually qualified by the words "for the purposes of the act". If we go through the rulings of the Supreme Court of Canada, the appeal courts of the provinces, the Tariff Board and the Anti-dumping Tribunal, we will see this same pattern recurring regarding mix-ups and misunderstandings of definitions.
If we pursue the matter further through regulations and rulings, we will find another maze of meanings which could be shaded, tilted, twisted or made to stick merely by adding the words "for the purposes of the act". For example, if the words "for the purposes of the act" were put in, we could say that all apples are oranges-and that is just about the way some things happen.
Some rulings have no statutory or regulatory authority. They are departmental rulings whose authorities are ministerial memos. This is where Lome Shields ran afoul of Revenue Canada. Mr. Shields called himself a manufacturer. Revenue Canada's excise division called him a manufacturer of bicycles and gave him an excise tax licence. He was allowed to import $100,000 worth of production equipment duty-free because it was to be used to manufacture bicycles. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce said he was a manufacturer and allowed him to label the product "Made in Canada". Canada Manpower gave him a $15,000 grant to teach new employees to manufacture bicycles. Statistics Canada considered Lome Shields a sporting goods manufacturer. The Ontario department of labour classed him as a manufacturer.
But Mr. Shields had not reckoned with a National Revenue dominion customs appraiser, Mr. John Peillard, who was doing his job. Mr. Peillard decided that Mr. Shields was an assembler of bicycles and thereby levied a 17.5 per cent duty on all parts he imported for his bicycles. In spite of the fact that all Mr. Shields' competitors were importing the same components duty free, Mr. Shields could not get Mr. Peillard to move from his decision. Mr. Peillard said that there was a ruling that 20 per cent Canadian content had to be evident before Mr. Shields could call himself a manufacturer. But he did not show the ruling to Mr. Shields. It was written, he said, in a ministerial memo, and that memo was confidential.
I told hon. members that I believe Mr. Shields had pre-sold a year's production based on an existing tariff under which manufacturers imported components duty free. To confound the matter further, it would have been possible, believe it or not, to import a complete bicycle at 16.5 per cent, and yet the components were bearing a 17.5 per cent duty. However, Mr. Shields' plan was to increase his Canadian content gradually as his market grew. He could offer subcontractors sufficient volumes to warrant tooling for certain components.
An uncontrollable hidden factor was foreign exchange. The dollar was unstable against most European and Asian currencies, but Shields did not know that was to play a part in the calculation of the 20 per cent Canadian content. If the dollar went down, the Canadian content would decline. Revenue Canada could then collect 17.5 per cent, assuming he reached
the 20 per cent. So aside from competition in the marketplace, all the problems of starting up a manufacturing company, training people, arranging financing and so forth, Mr. Shields had to deal with a confidential ruling, the contents of which could not be revealed to him, which would add a 17.5 per cent duty to several components he used in the manufacture of his product. The Revenue Canada official told him that the ruling was in a ministerial memo which was confidential. He could not see the memo, he could be told only the gist of it; but even if Mr. Shields was able to prove Canadian content, he still had to contend with the Canadian dollar. A drop in the dollar would cause the tariff to be imposed.
There was a further penalty. The Revenue Canada official had the final say as to what constituted 20 per cent Canadian content. For instance, he would not allow freight, overhead, packaging or profit to be part of the cost.
In a country which is crying out for manufacturing and which has a terrible current account and balance of payments problem, can hon. members believe that a manufacturer would, could or should have to jump through these hoops in order to do business?
Of course, the result of the imposition of the 17.5 per cent duty on the imported components of Mr. Shields' bicycles meant that a calculated profit became a loss. Customs duties of $310,000 meant that on every bicycle produced money was lost. After a period of time Mr. Shields' bankers decided they could no longer finance the operation. Applications were made by Mr. Shields to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce for assistance under the enterprise development program, but they came to nothing because the EDP had already mounted a $7.5 million rescue mission respecting CCM. What Mr. Shields did not know was that part of the deal was that the program would not fund an operation competing with CCM.
As Mr. Shields twisted and dangled on the bureaucratic string, various government departments were sealing his fate. He appealed to the then minister of national revenue, who is now a senator in the other place. The then minister saw the injustice. He could see that an even-handed approach to the problem was not being taken. He told Mr. Shields he would sort out the details and write to him. After numerous telephone calls to the minister, Shields received a letter prepared by the bureaucracy over the minister's signature which told him that no help would be forthcoming. The $310,000 customs duty had done its job. Seeing no relief, the banks placed Harry D. Shields Limited in receivership.
Lome Shields was not finished, however. He launched an appeal to the Tariff Board and, some 20 months later, the board heard his case. I recommend that everyone read this case. It is appeal No. 1498 and was heard October 8 and 9 of 1979. The Tariff Board ruled that there was no regulatory or statutory basis for the 20 per cent Canadian content, and Revenue Canada had to refund the duties levied against Mr. Shields' company. What that meant was that $230,000 was sent to the receiver in bankruptcy, and a further $80,000 in customs duties was cancelled. But it was too late. Harry D.
June 2, 1981

Shields Limited was closed. It was bankrupt. Approximately one hundred people lost their jobs. Several suppliers went unpaid, and the tragedy is that an enterprise which came out of the shoot alive and kicking was to die because of the stupidity and rigidity of the bureaucracy. Somebody decided that CCM would live and that Harry D. Shields would be strangled in the web of the bureaucracy.
What happened to Lome Shields? He lost his business. In order to live he sold most of his personal assets. He had a nervous breakdown. His father had a stroke which the doctors say was a direct result of stress and the bankruptcy of the business. The Department of National Revenue held $230,000 of Lome Shields' money for more than two years. The government used that money. When the Tariff Board said there was no statutory or regulatory basis for collecting the $230,000, the government returned the money, but no interest was paid. It was just a cheque in an envelope.
We hear much in this House about justice, about helping those who cannot help themselves, about the just society, about participatory democracy and about a charter of rights. Well, just ask Lome Shields how he feels about those cheap slogans which were born in an advertising office to adorn a speech or an election platform but, when put to the test, were cold and meaningless.
To Lome Shields, there is no democracy in Canada. If a bureaucrat decides you are to be taxed, you are taxed whether it is legal or not. Lome Shields learned that we are not all equal. If your business has loans guaranteed by the government, then you are more equal than a competitor who does not have those guarantees.
To the government, the competition policy means that the government eliminates competition from those who might challenge a company with loans guaranteed by the government, as they did with Harry D. Shields Ltd. And what happened to Mr. Peillard, the Dominion Customs appraiser? He was transferred to the electrical industry sector. One hundred people lost their jobs.
This is not, Mr. Speaker, an isolated case. There are many more people who have been turned off by imprecise definitions that vary from statute to statute, regulation to regulation. That is why I urge the government members to support our amendments and then follow through by placing the definitions of "manufacturing", "assembling", "processing" and "producing" before the committee of this House for resolution. Let us make a move against the bureaucracy so we will not have a repeat of the Lome Shields affair.
There are untold numbers of businessmen in Canada who live in fear of the government bureaucracy. Those businessmen and thousands more who will follow them are part of the solution to the economic problem we face. They are part of the solution to the unemployment problem. More than one million unemployed Canadians want that problem solved.
Businessmen who live in fear of the bureaucracy will tell you horror stories. When I asked some of them: "Why do you not
Excise Tax
speak out?" one of them replied: "Look, I do not want a tax job done on me". That is pretty shattering. When I tried to establish that is not the way Revenue Canada operates, this is what they replied: "Those guys have all the definitions and regulations and rulings, and they twist and turn them to suit the statutes and regulations". And then he went on the say: "For example, take the term 'manufacturing' "-the very thing we are talking about today. You see, Mr. Speaker, it comes back from many sources. If the government believes that a competitive market serves the consumer best, it will take a new look at many of the regulations and procedures.
When the bureaucracy acts in such a way that it makes loans, grants or loan guarantees to one industry and then hassles that industry's competitors, it effectively eliminates any choice for the consumer, and that is what happened to Lome Shields. He knew the market, he knew what would sell, he was trying to serve that market but he was frustrated in his endeavours.
There are many ways to handle the situation. The government could have said, as they did to the automobile industry, "Here is your Canadian content; we want a commitment from you that you will increase the Canadian component value on a schedule so that you will work toward an increasing Canadian content over a period of time". However, regardless of the method, it must be evenhanded. There is a constant battle over tariff rules and interpretations. You might recall a few months ago a number of businessmen from Manitoba descended on Ottawa because they had to pay a higher rate of duty on automotive products in their part of Canada than did businessmen in the same trade in Ontario. And this was just the result of an interpretation by people at the port of entry.
I have put forward to the members of the government a proposal that they do not support the change in the definition of "manufacturing", that they urge the minister to withdraw this section and refer it to a standing committee of this House, and that we begin to sort out the definitions of "manufacturing", "assembling", "processing" and "producing". You see, Mr. Speaker, I have confidence that we in this House have sufficient talent on all sides to solve this problem. I would like us to do that and to hand it back to the bureaucracy with the intruction that these are the definitions that they must use, and to get on with it.
In conclusion, let me say there are those who believe that there are two continuous struggles in this country. One is between the political parties whose ideology may differ, and there is an opportunity, as we know, to sort that out at election time. However, the real battle is between the government bureaucracy and the elected representatives of the people, and that is the battle we all must begin to fight. The bureaucracy is best served when the political battle is hot and when the party in power has a passive back bench.
I have issued the challenge, Mr. Speaker, to the government members. Now let us see if they are equal to the challenge and the task.

June 2, 1981

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am greatly saddened by many parts of Bill C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act. Time does not permit me to expose all of the almost punitive provisions that are contained in this act. However, I will focus in on one of the greediest parts of the bill.
I should say at the outset that I am astounded by the lack of feeling and understanding shown by the Liberal government in its attempt to index taxes on beer, wine and spirits. By no means am I suggesting that the Liberal government has probably driven thousands of Canadians to drink-maybe it has. Rather, my message is that the Liberals are discriminating against those Canadians who do like to partake every once in a while. With this hew and unprecedented indexing of taxes on beer, wines and spirits, Canadians can expect to pay up to $23.64 for a case of beer. This is a disgraceful increase of close to 160 per cent. Not only does the government seem to want to drive the cost of everyday goods and services up and up, but it also appears to want to soak Canadians for every penny it can get.
The government has been hearing a great deal lately from the opposition about inflation; and well they should. Inflation at 12.6 per cent, a new modern day record, is not a record that the Liberals should be proud of. The problem is, however, that the Grits seem bent on stimulating, not slowing down, this rapid climb toward world fame and lack of fortune. What does this mean for the average working Canadian? It means their dollar buys about one third as much as it did in 1971. They must pay about 7 per cent more for normal borrowing privileges than they had to pay when the Conservatives were in power. They have to pay about 60 cents more per gallon for gasoline and they are paying 15.2 per cent more just to eat than they had to pay last year. Now the Liberals are asking average Canadians to turn their pockets inside out and empty them just to buy a bottle of beer. When are the Grits going to get off the backs of the little guy and girl? That is a good question and I will give some of the answers right now.
The Liberals only have one solution to their years and years of overspending. They must raise more revenues to pay for their blank cheque spending habits. They will force average Canadians to fork over more and more money through a hidden tax which will be tacked on year after year, with no parliamentary say or control over it, and this is a very dangerous precedent.
The finance minister has said that the tax to be applied to this "all-beverage" class is simply a percentage tax and is therefore like many other levies imposed by the government. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a percentage tax. It is not, as the minister has claimed in this House, an ad valorem tax. In the strict sense an ad valorem tax is a constant percentage of the total sale price which is tacked on year after year. This percentage tax is changed only after all-party consultation and parliamentary voting has taken place.
This new scheme which is being deviously plotted by the Liberals would result in a submerged tax which would be indexed to the CPI rate of the all-beverage group. This means that whenever the price of production, the price of raw materials, the price of marketing, or any other price indicator, goes up by a certain percentage, the tax on the beverage will go up by a corresponding amount. This will amount to a piling
June 2, 1981

on of taxes and, eventually, will probably force one of the government's main income earners out of business.
Indexation does not necessarily have to be a bad thing. For example, indexation of personal income tax was introduced at the request of Mr. Robert Stanfield to protect taxpayers from inflation and to attempt to instil in the government better fiscal management and discipline. The government was not to profit from inflation by automatically collecting higher revenues from people because they obtained cost of living increases to keep up with inflation. By indexing personal income tax the government forced itself to manage the economy better, so that it could collect more revenue based on real wage gains. As members know, the government has been trying hard to do away with indexation of personal income tax and we in the official opposition have been trying to stop it.
By indexing taxes on spirits the government is managing to do exactly the opposite of what indexation of personal income tax is doing. It is taking advantage of a formula which is meant to protect the consumer against inflation and fiscal mismanagement. Through the indexation of taxes on goods the government can not only protect its revenues but will be taxing people on inflation and doing it without referring the matter to Parliament. It will also be creating a thicker smokescreen which will hide from public scrutiny its lack of policies to fight inflation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has said that this is just another percentage tax. I would like to tell the minister something of the percentages ordinary Canadians must work with now. When citizens want to buy a home- something about which every Canadian has dreamed but because of Liberal policies will probably never achieve-they must pay close to 20 per cent mortgage rates. Those people who are renewing their two, four or five-year mortgages will be stampeded into paying twice as much per month as they paid in the past. If they are overwhelmed by this excess burden they must sell their dream home or have the banks foreclose on them. This has been the case in Toronto recently, where over
3,000	people have been literally booted out of their homes because of high interest rates. It is no wonder ordinary Canadians need the odd drink just to settle their nerves. But now the Grits will deny them that choice, too.
Here is another percentage for the Minister of Finance to ponder awhile. Since 1960 bankruptcies have gone up by a totally unacceptable 758 per cent. These numbers do not even include businesses which collapsed but did not make use of the Bankruptcy Act, those which were placed in receivership, liquidated by secured creditors, or those which simply closed up shop because they could no longer cope. It is no wonder thousands of workers and a multitude of businesses are fleeing for their financial lives to the United States.
I should add here that this financial bastion for Canadian businesses may soon be closing its doors. This, of course, is due to the preferential treatment given to Canadian firms over American firms in the National Energy Program. The Liberals are causing a backlash in the United States which will begin taking its toll on Canadian firms shortly if the energy program
Excise Tax
is not abandoned soon. The end result will be that Canadian firms will have no place left to go. They will have migrated to the United States where the economic and political climate is more favourable. They will be stifled there, too, because American firms in Canada have received such a beating from the Liberal government. This is reciprocity in quite a different form, for which we only have the Grits to blame.
I would like to return to the matter of bankruptcies for a moment. There have been some 27,000 personal bankruptcies since the beginning of 1980. How can the Liberals even think of adding insult to injury by putting beer, wine and spirit prices out of reach? What other commodity will they try to index in the future?
It seems that the Liberals are desperate for cash. Only now do they realize that they have grossly overstepped their spending bounds. Only now do they realize that the Progressive Conservative Party was perfectly right in its policy of reducing the NDP-Liberal created deficit. Only now will the Liberal party attempt to cut their expenditures to an acceptable level.
Now, though, they are using every and any means they can to extort money from the average Canadian. This money grabbing begins at the provincial level where the Grits are trying to finagle profits made on resources by western provinces through new equalization schemes. Of course, the provinces quickly saw through this federal ploy and they are fighting tooth and nail to save their new-found riches. Therefore, the Grits have once again created division in the country. First, there was the Constitution, then the National Energy Program and now there is the equalization scheme. Along the way they batter average Canadians by imposing hidden taxes on beverages.
The money grabbing continues. We see in this bill new taxes on oil and gas. The devastating effects that these new taxes will have on the oil and gas sector, as well as on the energy service sector, have been excellently explained by many of my colleagues in the debate yesterday and in the debate on this bill on Tuesday last. Therefore, I will restrict my comments to motion 22 in this bill.
At the outset of my remarks I described the indexation of taxes as being discriminatory. It is not discriminatory simply because of its adverse effects on the average working Canadian, but also because of the way it applies to the various items in the all-beverage subgroup.
During committee hearings the Minister of Finance entertained briefs from the Brewers Association of Canada. These briefs showed clearly that the result of excise levies introduced in April, 1980 was to initiate a swing from beer and wine to hard liquor. This is clearly demonstrated by facts and figures. The annual percentage change in sales for beer, wine and distilled spirits between 1974 and 1980 was 1.7 per cent, 8.3 per cent and 3.3 per cent respectively. After the announcement of the excise levies in 1980 the percentage change in sales for the April, 1980 to January, 1981 period was negative 3.6 per cent for beer, negative 1.8 per cent for wine and positive 4.6 per cent for spirits. During the committee hearings the minister said it was neither his intention nor his job to influence the
10180

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
alcoholic beverage choice of Canadians. Nonetheless, the effect of his April, 1980 announcement was to discourage the consumption of beer and wine in favour of the consumption of hard liquor, as can be seen in the figures 1 have quoted.
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, the April, 1980 announcements included sharp and unprecedented excise levy increases of 29 per cent for beer and 155 per cent for wine, compared with a nominal increase of only 6 per cent for distilled spirits. The result was substantially to reduce the relative tax burden on distilled spirits compared to beer. If the unintentional shift in consumption choices from beer to distilled spirits is to be corrected, then the traditional relationship should be restored by increasing the levy on distilled spirits by a proportionate amount. If the shift in consumption from low to high alcoholic content beverages is not reversed, the economic impact on the brewing industry and on agricultural producers who depend on the brewing industry will be severe. In addition, the negative impact on jobs will be significant, as the production and distribution of beer and wine are much more labour-intensive than similar operations for spirits.
As an example of the potentially negative impact on jobs, I would like to quote from a speech given by my hon. friend for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). He said:
-the wineries and the grape growers employ over 18,000 persons. Is not that a segment of the community worth considering? In its brief to the standing committee, the Canadian Wine Institute hit the nail on the head when it stated that neither winemaking nor grape growing is a profitable business.
For the information of members of this House let us say that in so far as wine production is concerned, the net return is less than 5 per cent of the capital cost investment. That is not a great venture from a profit-making point of view. There are already declining sales and, thanks to that earlier 155 per cent increase in the excise tax announced last April, this cannot fail to continue as the government loads quarterly increases onto the retail cost of wine. With this decline will come the collapse of the smaller wine industries-the cottage wine industries-which have improved the taste and quality of domestic wines. It will also lead to lay-offs in the larger wine industries.
This is but one example of what a seemingly minute tax can do to a thriving industry.
Furthermore, there is overwhelming evidence showing that a higher incidence of alcohol-related health problems, crime and accidents is related to a relatively higher level of distilled spirits consumption. This factor in itself should be sufficient to convince policymakers of the dangers involved in encouraging, through the tax system, the increased consumption of hard liquor. No country has ever set out to use the tax system to encourage, via the price mechanism, the shift in consumption patterns toward hard liquor and away from naturally brewed and fermented products such as beer, wine and cider; in fact, a number of countries have done exactly the opposite.
The proposal to index alcoholic beverage excise levies should be automatically dropped in favour of continuing to seek changes to rates of these taxes and duties by having them approved by Parliament as part of the traditional budgetary process. It is my feeling that most ordinary Canadians believe that government is there to serve and protect them in a reasonable and responsible fashion. This means that Canadians believe that, through debate and the normal voting procedure, decisions and policies are made which will serve to better society as a whole. This tax completely violates both the trust which Canadians have put in the system and the system itself.
During committee consideration the minister stated he did not believe indexing would affect the stability of the industry. However, one of the effects of the indexing scheme is that it would exacerbate the sales situation existing since the excise levy increases of April, 1980. Soon the price of two dozen bottles of beer will have increased by 157 per cent, as I stated earlier. The price of a 25-ounce bottle of inexpensive gin will increase by only 101 per cent. Obviously, this will further accelerate the shift in consumption patterns to hard liquor and away from beer and wine.
I will conclude my statements by calling on the Minister of Finance to eliminate this section of Bill C-57 which will index taxes on beer, wine and spirits to the CPI rate for all beverages and for once get off the back of the little guy who, by far, will suffer the most if this provision is approved.

speechtext:
I would like to turn to the second part of this bill, which is a tax on natural gas and natural gas liquids. As everyone in this House is aware, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stood in his place and said; "We have no intention of taxing natural gas, of putting a tax on natural gas exported to the United States". Then he turned right around and said: "We are going to tax all natural gas in Canada, whether it is consumed domestically or exported". As everyone is aware, the appeal court of Alberta recently ruled against the federal government taxing another government, namely, the government of Alberta. This is dealt with in a section of the British North America Act. This case has now been appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada. Hopefully the Supreme Court of Canada will render a decision on the side of the producing provinces.
The petroleum gas tax or revenue tax is clearly a tax on provincial resources. We and all of the provinces understand this to be illegal. I will probably come back to this point when the bill comes up for the third reading because I question whether we should discuss this bill on third reading. As I understand it, we are simply reporting the bill to the House, but there is a question in my mind as to whether we should actually be discussing certain parts of this bill while they are before the Supreme Court of Canada.
I would like to draw attention to something which is pretty important. Total exports of natural gas in 1978 were approximately 882 billion cubic feet. In 1979, under a Conservative government, exports rose to one trillion cubic feet. In 1980, under a Liberal government, they again declined to 800 billion cubic feet, which is the lowest total exports in the last five years. In addition, natural gas exports in 1978, in dollar terms, were $2.2 billion; in 1979, $3.1 billion; in 1980, $4 billion, in spite of a decrease in volume. Basically, the reason is that we tie the price of exports of natural gas to the price of imported oil. Even though they are unrelated, this government has a formula whereby it ties the two together. Therefore, we cannot export as much gas as we want. The government would be receiving $1.5 billion annually if it did not tie the price of natural gas to the price of imported oil. Of course, once again it is anxious not to give Alberta anything more than it possibly can. I cannot help but think how our balance of payments would be helped with that $1.5 billion per year, and I cannot help but think what it would do for interest rates in Canada if an additional $1.5 billion was coming in.
The natural gas companies in western Canada, which are mostly in Alberta, have stated that they could export 50 per cent more gas than they are allowed to at present if they could take it out of the ground and had a market for it. It is quite evident that many of these companies will go broke. These are average-sized Canadian companies which cannot get their natural gas out of the ground for at least five years. When they go to the bank they can only borrow funds to 25 per cent of real value. They cannot sell their gas because it is shut in by the policies of the government. They cannot export that gas.
Excise Tax
I should like now to come to what I consider to be an unbelievable tax which the government is going to introduce on wine, beer, spirits and tobacco. I am not opposed to a tax on any of these products but I am opposed to a tax which is indexed and which will automatically increase as inflation does. This is the first tax that the government will use on industry in general. If it gets away with this, we can expect that the tax on all items will be indexed against inflation. You and I, Mr. Speaker, will pay tax in future on every item we buy and that tax will be indexed to inflation. This is just the first step and I shall come back to it briefly in my conclusion.
I should like now to deal with Part IV of Bill C-57, which imposes an 8 per cent tax on petroleum and gas revenues. This is a tax at the wellhead and can also be interpreted as a tax on provincial resources. It will affect exploration and development by the whole petroleum industry. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stood in this House and said that drilling is not declining. Every week and month last fall he told us that. He said that there was a surplus of oil rigs and that drilling companies were expanding because they anticipated an expansion of exploration and development. That did not come about because of the national energy policy, Mr. Speaker. There are now only 50 per cent of the rigs operating in Canada that were operating one year ago. Approximately $2 billion is flowing out of the country each year and will continue to do so for the next five years because of the national energy policy.
In the province of Saskatchewan one company shut down 190 wells within the last five months and another company shut down 125 wells. This begs the question, how could they possibly shut down producing wells? It is very simple. It was because they were losing money. Even though they are not allowed to shut wells down, they simply wait until the wells need repairs and then do not repair them. The repairs are put off indefinitely. This practice will continue until we notice a drop in production from these marginal wells. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources continue to hold that this will not happen and that it is not happening. I could give the names of companies, Mr. Speaker, but I shall not embarrass them.
It is interesting that the oil industry raises 70 per cent of its funds internally while the utilities, most of which are owned by governments, raise less than 50 per cent of their capital internally. That is a turn around for the industry. The cash flow of the oil and gas industry in Canada has been reduced by 20 per cent to 40 per cent on account of the policies of the government which wants to control the oil industry.
I could go on and tell why this is being done, Mr. Speaker. I have said, as have others in this House before, that if anyone really wants to know what kind of Canada we will have in future, they should read the writings of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He is nothing but a socialist. Any communist will tell you that the socialists are the tool of the communist party, of the communist world.
