I hear to my left the pinko Peter Pan of politics. He has had his opportunity to speak on this bill. He does not disagree with what I am saying about the socialists; he just thinks it is funny.
1 should like to quote briefly from a brief submitted to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs by the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada. On page 9 of the brief there appears the following passage:
We are mindful of the government's intention to direct three objectives of the National Energy Program, namely:
1)	Security of supply and the ultimate independence from the world oil
market;
2)	A fair pricing and revenue sharing regime; and
3)	Greater ownership and control of the oil and gas industry.
The Minister of Finance has stated that "That two taxes contained in this Bill are essential for the achievement of these objectives.''
It is the position of the Independent Petroleum Association that the first objective, that of security or supply, is not possible under this Fiscal regime ... It is also our contention that a fair price and revenue sharing program that places the Canadian oil and gas industry in Financial jeopardy to continue in Canada when more attractive foreign opportunities exist, is not conducive to future exploration and development in this country. Lastly, the ownership and control objective as stated by the minister has no place in an Excise Tax Act.
Mr. Speaker, this is submitted by an association of companies which are Canadian controlled, not foreign controlled, and which are moving to the United States. It is not the case that I cannot find Liberals to agree with this, but they are prepared to say: "We are going to change it in the future and it won't be that bad". But it is already that bad. Everyone should be aware that it will take two to five years to bring back the oil rigs that have gone to the United States.
The IPAC group concludes with this question:
Is it then the intention of the government to enact selective tax legislation for every segment of the industrial base at some time in the future?
That being the case, the stability of the entire business and investment community will be in question. If it is not the intent of the government, why should tax laws be enacted which are so clearly discriminatory to one sector? That is the essence. It is a tax not upon one industry but upon all industries. This bill is a tax not upon one segment of the economy but upon all segments of the economy.
I shall summarize some of the items in Bill C-57. The national energy policy, which really brought about this bill, has reduced the cash flow of the oil and gas companies by 20 per cent to 40 per cent. Their earnings have been decreased by 60 per cent to 70 per cent.
This is a tax which does not approach earnings normally by simply taxing profits. The government does not want to do that. The government wants to tax these companies before they make profits.
This is a bill which does not help our balance of payments problems. It does not do one thing to help our balance of payments. This bill does not do one thing to help the deficit of Canada. We hear the Liberals telling us that they are going to reduce the deficit. How can the government reduce the deficit
when it buys oil companies which do not produce one more barrel of oil? Money is leaving Canada. How is our deficit being helped when Canadian companies are taking their money across the border to the United States? There are companies in Canada doing nothing else but raising funds for Canadian companies that operate in the United States. As I mentioned before, approximately $2 billion a year is being raised for this purpose.
This is a bill which goes one step further toward government ownership of business in this country. Of course, the government likes to cloud the horizon by saying it is not trying to take over all business. Of course not. But if hon. members read the writings of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), they will find that he wants to control everything. Having 51 per cent will control all businesses in Canada. Last week, I believe, in Montreal the Prime Minister said: "All businesses in Canada at one time or another will have to come to the government for assistance". What a ridiculous statement to make. Of course, we know how ridiculous he is after listening to him during question period. I would be ashamed to belong to the same party as anyone making a statement like that. This is a statement with which the Liberals will have to live forever.
We regard this bill, this tax on industry, as punitive. If that is not a strong enough word to describe it, then I say it is vindictive. This government is out to get industry and private enterprise because the government wants to socialize or nationalize, if you will, industry in Canada.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright) in his closing comment said that the government is out to get private enterprise and entrepreneurs. I maintain the government is out to get Canadians generally. The government does not select; it wants to get everybody.
June 2, 1981

I am delighted to speak to Bill C-57, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act. I would call it an act of confiscation. In the days since this bill was brought before the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has been heard to say that if injury of significant disadvantage is experienced by any group, he would remove the burden in the subsequent budget.
Those are lovely words, but who is the minister kidding? He is not fooling me nor is he fooling the public. Once that government grabs a little bit of money, it hangs on for dear life to it because it is known that this government never gives it back. The government's game is to take more and more and more. This government has no intention of rescinding anything it presents to this House.
I believe that the 8 per cent energy tax is totally immoral and is probably the most damaging tax imposed in Canada. It is not only destroying the possibility of self-sufficiency in the oil industry, it is destroying the Canadian economy. It is being felt in Ontario, Quebec and the eastern provinces. With this government's spending spree, it is obvious it loves to feed the inflation fire. That is the key problem in Canada today because it is ravaging the life of all Canadians.
This government, through the National Energy Program, has not only written off the western potential, the western spirit, the western hope, but has completely desecrated the Canadian economy. This government is more interested in buying service stations, maybe for the real estate, and oil from Mexico than in encouraging, through appropriate tax relief, oil production in Canada. This government will be so overcome by greed that it will dry up the source of supply, similar to what happens to a poorly managed dairy farm.
The wellhead tax on the production of gas and petroleum products is a cannibalization of not only the petroleum industry but the producer and the Canadian public. In Canada the price of gasoline has increased 60 cents since this government took over, all of which increase has gone into the government's coffers. Europeans pay $4.50 a gallon. Although a great deal of that price goes into government coffers, it pays for imported oil because the Europeans do not have the possibility of self-sufficiency. In this country, at the rate this government is going, I would say that in two or three years gasoline will cost $9 a gallon or $2 a litre. But the producer in the west will get nothing from any rise in price, nor will Canadian industry. All the funds will flow back into Ottawa. That is the government's game. Its plan is not to pay back loans from other people but to spend money.
Governments are elected, in theory, to tailor spending programs to revenues. This government throws out that theory; that is of no concern to it. It theorizes, not knowing how much it will take in, that everything it takes in will be given away, along with everything else we will have in the next 20 years. The government grabs money from every source it can. It is a wonder it has not jumped on the western farmer and the Ontario farmer. Their prices have gone up. Next it may place an indexed tax on wheat and really destroy this economy. That is the only thing we have left. We have no industy. Nothing
Excise Tax
has been done to encourage industry in this country. The government has created a complete division in this country.
Originally, under the British North America Act that is now being rescinded any royalty on resources belonged to the provinces. This tax inflicts upon the provinces a wound that will be deep and will have significance for many years to come. The federal government has the right to raise all the taxes it wants by a revision to the Income Tax Act. It could follow a logical system of raising money.
I said before in this House that maybe it is time to get some imaginative plagiarism of taxes from other countries, for example for building up industry. The United States had the same problem with the multinational oil companies. They put on a windfall profits tax which had a beginning and an end. In essence, it was indexed so that each year the windfall profits tax became less. It was a smaller percentage of the sale price of the fuel. We have never come up with an original program like that. We just hammer the citizens of this country over the head with a two by four. We do not use logic and we destroy the country in the process.
The Liberals love going to the trough. That is their expertise-they go to the trough and get all they can. If they want to get a lot out of the trough, I will tell them how to do it. Put the price of oil up to 75 per cent of the world price. Put on a windfall profits tax. Then watch the development in this country. Watch the industrial base in Ontario grow. The federal government will get more money than it ever dreamed of. Ontario will survive. My riding would benefit, as would Quebec and the maritimes.
We are only kidding ourselves. By the time we get up to 75 per cent of the world price, the government will take so much of that price there will be nothing left for the producer. I say put the price up now, put on a windfall profits tax and abolish this 8 per cent tax which cannot even be deducted from your profit and loss account. The petroleum industry would benefit, the drilling rigs would come back into Canada, service industries would develop and people would be employed in the west and in Ontario. The entire economy of this country would get moving from coast to coast. The automobile manufacturers in Scarborough will again be busy building trucks. That plant is now shut down about five days out of ten. Why? Who in the west can afford to buy trucks when there is no revenue coming in?
The government's greed is absolutely incredible. It recently put up the export tax because it is short of money and we have a balance of payments problem. Why not drop the tax and allow more products to be exported across the border? More revenue will flow back into Canada. It will come back into the hands of the producers and service industries which the government has the right to tax.
Export our products to those who want them. The Americans want our gas but at a reasonable price. Every time we sell our product, it leads to exploration for new gas. New oil will also be found. When you drill for gas, you do not know

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
whether you will hit gas or oil. Therefore, more oil and gas will be brought on stream. Oil and gas from the north will come on stream much faster. At present we may have to wait 50 years before this oil comes on stream.
This government follows the easy way of bringing in oil-at the expense of the taxpayers. If this government were really sensible, it would bring back depreciation allowances, exploration expenses and development expenses which could be written off. I suggest it get rid of its petroleum incentive program. It is a joke. In fact, it states in an amendment that it is a joke. The government says that if you choose not to take the incentive program, you can deduct the amount you would get from your 8 per cent royalty tax. That is just money going through the system, that is all it is. It does not give anything to the oil industry. Everything that is given to them is taken away. In effect, you are putting them in the position of a possible 30 per cent negative cash flow. You are not giving them anything and the government is losing everything. It is losing revenue on the income of taxpayers throughout Canada.
We must get rid of the National Energy Program and the 8 per cent royalty. The government calls it an excise tax, but I call it a royalty because that is what it is. The government says it wants to Canadianize the industry. I accept that. I believe that is sound. At least some companies have worked hard to do this under this incentive, but it could have been done in a much better way which would have put us in a better light in the eyes of other countries.
This incentive of a depletion allowance, exploration and development expenses should apply to Canadian companies only. Believe me, Mr Speaker, it would get money out of the banks and back to work in this country. What has flowed south across the border will come back into Canada. The drilling rigs will return to this country and the economy will be booming. However, this government wants to hold this country down. I do not understand the reason for it, but they are against anything of a positive nature.
This excise tax hits the people of my riding. The government is putting indexation on the last pleasure of the working man. High interest rates are slowly but surely eroding his home base. He does not know if he can hang on to his house. The tragedy is the indexing of the tax on beer. I refer specifically to beer. It will never be a tax with representation. This tax on beer will never come before this House of Commons. We will never be able to speak on this tax again, nor the tax on wine and spirits.
The working man who works from eight to four of five can no longer afford many pleasures because of the inflation brought about by this government. Now the government is taking away his last pleasure. He is again being hit over the head by a two by four.
I am told it is to protect government revenues derived as a result of this tax from erosion. What about the erosion of the working man's pleasure? What about the erosion of his income? What is the government doing to the working Canadian? It is stripping him of his last pleasure. He is not only being hit with excessive income tax, but now the little bit
of money he has left in his pocket to buy a small case of beer at the end of the week is being taken away from him.
Perhaps the government is dedicated to solving the problem of alcoholism in this country, I do not know. But I do know one thing about this measure. The government will lose more than it will gain because there are still many people with initiative in this country who will start to produce their own beer in their basements. Who could afford to pay $22 for 12 pints of beer, which I understand will be the price in about 1988? The government is taking away homes with high interest rates and it is now taking away the average man's beer. What are you going to do with that man on the street? This reminds me very much of what happened in Germany in the 1930s. People lost their homes, they began to starve, and then a powerful dictator came along to solve all their problems. God help us so that that does not happen here in this country.
I believe the indexing of the tax on beer is totally immoral and is a concept totally the reverse of that which Robert Stanfield had when he suggested the indexing of income tax. Indexing of income tax was meant to protect the working man against inflation and fiscal mismanagement, the cause of inflation. The government is now going to reverse that concept. The minister keeps talking about the next budget when he will take indexing out. I think the government had better start indexing itself because the government keeps taking money in.
I received an advertisement today which talks about a sudsidy of $800 to reduce consumption of petroleum products. The government is going to give each Canadian citizen $800. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that the government will have to borrow that $800 in Switzerland at 15 per cent interest rate, compounded over 5.5 years, which will mean it will have to pay back $1,600? Furthermore, the money will be taken away from the taxpayer to pay that loan back.
Why does this government not get to work, instead of continually increasing taxes, to find ways of cutting taxes and protecting the working Canadian? He is being rubbed the wrong way and pushed too far. This government is on a binge. This is the only way it can control Canadians, by taking everything away from them.
While we are talking about inflation, which I referred to as basically resulting from mismanagement by this government over the last 13 years, let me point out that in a recent Gallup poll 65 per cent of Canadians indicated approval of severe reductions in government spending, similar to what is taking place south of the border. They are talking about general reductions, and the majority of people expect a positive effect on the Canadian economy and our inflation. Instead of always coming to the trough here trying to get more money, why do members across the way not sit back in their offices and try to figure out how to cut spending?
The next part of this bill deals with small weekly newspapers. The Kent commission has been currently trying to determine the detrimental effects of control of the press basically by three groups in this country, the Toronto Star, Southam and
June 2, 1981

Thomson. The Toronto Star stayed out of it because it has only one paper, but it is sold right across this country and it gets the Liberals elected every time. During the time the Kent commission has been questioning this monopoly control the government has been planning to fiit small weeklies, the independent press in this country which combats these large chains of newspapers. They are the only papers which can still tell the truth.
The government has now found a new tax with which to hit and hammer them over the head, like with a two by four. The government is going to tax those weeklies on all their advertising and the supplements they carry. Advertising and advertising inserts are how these newspapers manage to carry on. Most of these weeklies do not make a lot of money. They are operated by individual owners who are trying to make a buck in small towns. These small newspapers are the only defence we have in print against those three major papers everyone knows about.
I hope the minister will reverse these taxes when it is shown they are hurting some specific industries. I hope he will abolish this tax so as not to kill the small independent newspapers of this country. Members on that side think these advertisers can distribute their material through the mail. The trouble is that the inserts carried by these weekly newspapers come out on Wednesday for sales that take place on Thursday, Friday and Saturday. Can you imagine putting these inserts in the mail? By the time they got to us the sale would be over and the prices would be marked up 50 per cent. Furthermore, this would involve another tax on the public.
This whole measure is supposed to give the appearance of this government's efficient commerce. To me, the government has done an absolutely disastrous thing by bringing forward this tax. I can only hope that, as in my wildest dreams, we can in some way defeat the government on this measure, as 1 think it represents an absolute disaster to Canada, the west and our national economy.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to make some remarks about Bill C-57, presently before the Flouse, entitled "an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas".
Let me say at the outset that there are certain aspects of this bill, as with any piece of government legislation, which will be helpful to Canadians, in particular those that deal with exemptions from excise tax as set out under Part I. This party generally supports the nature of those exemptions, with a couple of exceptions.
We have proposed an amendment relating to the exemption for utensils, instruments and equipment used in university teaching and research. This party would like to see the adoption of a minor amendment to clause 12 of the bill which would rule out the requirement that such devices be specifically designed for research, thereby exempting all such equipment employed in the conduct of research and teaching up to 50 per
Excise Tax
cent of the time. We would recommend the removal of the reference to the word "design" in the second line of clause 12.
In addition, we feel that included in the list of fuel sales tax exemptions there ought to be an exemption on fuels used in pilot training. If one has regard for the tremendously increased cost that Canadians of all ages must anticipate if they want to enter into pilot training, with the new Revenue Canada ruling that will disallow any tax benefit for flying training time in excess of the first 35 hours it becomes very important that a certain measure be introduced to ensure that the practice of flight training is given as much consideration as are other aspects of vocational and academic training programs in this country.
With that said, I think it is fair to say that speakers for this party, and in many cases my colleagues in the party to the left, have taken extreme exception to numerous aspects of the proposed legislation in Bill C-57. As the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) pointed out a few minutes ago, this move toward indexation of revenue sources, whether it be federal or provincial, as in the case of the recent budget by the province of Ontario which included indexing of that province's revenue sources, is a very retrograde step. It seems to me governments are elected to serve the people, that the people of this country are not here to serve their governments. The practice of indexing income tax exemptions under the Income Tax Act must be retained and the government should not even begin to contemplate, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) has often implied, deindexation of exemptions under that act. In that way government does serve the needs of the people by ensuring that the timeless pace of inflation does not erode the basic minimum income people are entitled to enjoy tax free within this country.
On the other hand, the indexation of government revenue sources such as that proposed respecting the spirits, wine and tobacco provisions of Bill C-57, and the move by Ontario to index provincial gasoline tax revenue, really must be recognized as being inflationary because indexation, as in the case of the present bill, on a quarterly basis relating to the consumer price index component of cost arising from those particular consumables-the basic process of calculating an increased rate of tax revenue on an ad valorem basis rather than on a straight value basis-has an amplifying effect. If the revenue is tied to a certain percentage of the retail sales price of a particular commodity, then every time there is an increase in the tax to keep track of that indexing formula, it will have a reflected effect on the consumer price index and then will lead a quarter later to the need to index the rate of tax up once again. There is an amplifying effect which fuels inflation inherent in these provisions to index tax revenue sources to the consumer price index. Therefore it is wrong.
Of course, as many of my colleagues have pointed out, there is a change in balance between the excise tax rate assigned to certain spirits and to alcoholic beverages of 40 per cent alcoholic content or higher. Changing the ratio of taxation on

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
those alcoholic beverages compared with beer and wine leads to a situation in which people will ultimately be more inclined to buy hard alcoholic beverages as opposed to beer and wine. This is completely contrary to what is advocated by leading health and alcoholism authorities and to the practices of many other nations, most notably France, where in fact the rate of excise taxation against wine on a per unit alcohol basis is very, very much lower than against alcoholic spirits.
The brewing and wine-making industries made representations at the committee stage in opposition to this kind of indexing which, by the year 1991, I believe, could lead to Canadians paying some $26 for a 24-pack of beer compared with only $16 for a bottle of gin. The effect of that is quite obvious. The average Canadian making a visit to the liquor store is much more likely to buy hard alcoholic spirits than beer or wine.
As 1 said a few moments ago, the amplifying effect of this method fuels inflation because the rates of taxation are continually indexed upwards as the consumer price index rises, and the consumer price index will rise as tax revenues are increased. This is a very regressive measure and quite unacceptable to this party.
I want to talk for a short while about the energy aspects of Bill C-57, in particular the so-called natural gas and liquid natural gas tax provisions as set out in Part II of Bill C-57 and also the producers' tax and producer royalty provisions contained within Part IV of the bill.
Hon. members may recall that in the early autumn of 1980 a number of questions were asked of the government, and of the Minister of Finance in particular, as to whether he intended to introduce an export tax on natural gas. There were denials, most vehemently from the hon. Leader of the Government in the Senate, the senator from British Columbia, who pledged that there would be no such tax on British Columbia natural gas resources, as did the former leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia, Mr. Gordon Gibson.
In fact, hon. members may recall that over 32,000 residents of British Columbia sent in petitions to this House in the months of October and November opposing any tax on the export of natural gas and, by implication, on all forms of natural gas, whether exported or consumed within the province, because those are viewed by the residents of British Columbia, Alberta and the other western provinces as resources to which they are entitled under the provisions of the British North America Act and part of the deal under which British Columbia, willingly and happily, entered into confederation in 1871.
One might ask why the provinces are so anxious to maintain title to natural resources. The fact is that people, those in the more remote regions of Canada at least, are convinced they get better value for their tax dollar and for their resources by seeing those dollars invested and spent wisely and close to home by their municipal and provincial governments. Last autumn at the Union of British Columbia Municipalities meeting, the mayors of British Columbia unanimously opposed the imposition of a federal tax on the natural resources of
British Columbia because those resources and the revenues they are capable of earning ultimately translate into the building of schools, roads, facilities, services and employment opportunities for the people of British Columbia.
There is a big revenue grab coupled with what I call the big lie which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and his colleagues regularly put out about how wealthy the western resource-producing provinces are. I invite more hon. members on the government side to visit towns like Calgary and Edmonton in January or February, or at any time of the year, and to view the lack of sidewalks in my own community, the lack of closed drainage ditches, the lack of adequate, completed parks, the lack of adequate hospitals and the lack of adequate playground equipment and facilities. These things are enjoyed in Ontario and Quebec, the much more established part of Canada. We are building an infrastructure out there which this part of Canada has enjoyed for over a century, and this costs money.
Therefore, if the per capita income from natural resources is as large as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources often likes to proclaim-some $1,600 per person-he should be honest with the people of Canada and let them realize how large the per capita income is in other parts of this country which comes from manufacturing and industry. How large is the per capita income from government in the Ottawa area? How large is the per capita income in some of the less affluent parts of Canada because of government gratuities and redistribution under the formal procedure of equalization, to which all provinces agree? However, to go around perpetrating this big lie and proclaiming that the people of western Canada are greedy, selfish and too fat cat is absolutely intolerable to western Canadians. We invite the minister and others to travel to British Columbia, Alberta and elsewhere to see roads sliding down the sides of mountains. I invite them to travel to many of our backwoods areas where there is not the pavement there is in most parts of Ontario and Quebec.
Much building and investment must be carried out in western Canada, and western Canadians, thank you very much, would like to have more say about how those investments are made than the federal government believes is necessary. If they are not allowed, within the confines of confederation, to make those decisions, then we cannot fault western Canadians for looking for another way. There is a lack of trust. History has proved that the Liberal big spenders in Ottawa have no sense of value and no sense of thriftiness when it comes to reinvesting the great bounty we as Canadians all enjoy.
It is interesting to speculate as to why Alberta and Saskatchewan have heritage funds and why the province of British Columbia has a B.C. Resources Investment Corporation or a British Columbia Petroleum Corporation. Why is it that we are able to put something away for tomorrow and invest in the building and development of our future when the government in Ottawa is bankrupt and leading our country down the same road to absolute economic chaos?
I think the natural gas tax which has been levied through the budget and as reflected in Bill C-57 is nothing more than a
June 2, 1981

revenue grab. Then the government imposes an 8 per cent production tax and, in addition to that, a producers' royalty on people who actually pay royalties to others for investing in our oil and gas industry.
The negative effect of these provisions of the National Energy Program are visible everywhere in our country today. For example, I imagine the bureaucrats, cabinet ministers and government members who contemplated imposing an 8 per cent producers' tax did not bother to calculate the rate of return on investment to determine whether investors in western Canadian oil and gas exploration could absorb such a level of taxation. And, of course, the massive number of jobs being lost in western Canada, the migration of whole industries associated with drilling rigs heading south where the rate of return is much larger, is indicative of the fact that this government is incompetent to do a quantitative analysis of the consequences of its policies before implementation.
I imagine, Mr. Speaker, that the government did not consider that a higher tax on natural gas, starting at 30 cents a thousand cubic feet or 28 cents a gigagoule and rising to double that amount within two years, would have an impact on farmers or on the important production of synthetic fertilizer from natural gas. It has now had that fact brought to its attention by the federation of Alberta gas co-ops and other groups, who made representations to the effect that the food we eat is really produced from our natural resources and that any increase in cost to the producer will ultimately be reflected in the cost of living index.
Of course, this government in its budget imposed a tax across the board at the wellhead which has its impact on home heating fuels; but that is compounded in western Canada where most people rely on natural gas for heating and comfort, which is a change from the way it was when I was a small boy 30 years ago and we had no timber, just a bit of coal, and we certainly did not have the warmth and convenience of natural gas.
Then suddenly this government increases home heating costs to western Canadians, indeed to the people of Ontario and Quebec that burn natural gas, by some 33 per cent from last October until next winter. That is a cost which has to be borne by the old age pensioners. I had the residents of a Kiwanis subsidized housing project in my riding receive a surtax on their December heating bill and every subsequent month which comes directly out of their old age pension, the supplement and widows' benefits. That surtax arises out of the National Energy Program. The plastics which are so essential to our manufacturing industry, the plastics that we waste too much of in this country, are also being taxed excessively.
We are doing this to initiate a concept of nationalization of our major industries in the energy sector. We started with the Petro-Canada acquisition and pretended that Canada was buying an oil company, but of course we were borrowing money through the chartered banks by assigning the term preferred shares to the banks who, in turn, conveyed that trust
Excise Tax
to foreign lenders, which made it possible for Canada to attempt to purchase a major part of the Canadian petroleum industry.
We now have across Canada brand-new Petro-Canada service centres that western Canadians avoid like the plague. In shopping centres which are competing with established centres they are putting in pizza parlours, convenience stores and clothing stores, which is again an example of the kind of irritant that western Canadians feel. It is an Ottawa Liberal attempt to invade and intrude into private sector business principles and traditions in western Canada which is totally repugnant to western Canadians. Of course, that leads to the question of which Liberal fat cats get the leases on these spaces. How many of these smaller deals, much smaller than the one that Mr. Strong apparently profited from tremendously by setting up the acquisition of Petrofina for the government, are benefiting people who happen to be friends, backers or bagmen of the Liberal party?
The Grits and their corporate friends are reaping high profits, and I suggest it is high time the government and the people of Canada know where these profits from high interest rates are going. I suggest that the high interest rates and high rates of return on investments being earned in Canada are being sucked off by certain financial institutions, friends of the Liberal party, who we will see emerge as the new Power Corporations of the future which want to take control of our oil and gas industry because they have special access to government and cabinet. I will name names. I am thinking of the Campeaus, the Strongs, the Desmarais and the McCains. I do not know how much others there are but it would seem to me-and this is certainly an irritant to western Canadians- that these individuals prominently connected with the Liberal party are probably somehow linked to high interest rates and the profits being accrued therefrom, and to the power plays being made in an attempt to grab a controlling interest in the oil and gas industry in Canada, particularly in the offshore areas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate with a growing concern over the direction the government is taking with regard specifically to my region of the country, western Canada. It runs completely counter to the good of this region and thereby to the good of the entire country. The energy provisions in this bill are designed for short term financial benefits and narrow political gains in central Canada. In the long run they will be disastrous for both the economy and the political viability of this nation. The friction and ill feeling caused by these measures, not to mention the legal precedents being established daily, weekly and monthly in our courts, will in the long run fan the flames of western discontent to unmanageable proportions. Instead of a co-operative form of federalism, we will be faced with a never-ending series of confrontations between competing levels of government.

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
It is impossible to understand the consequences of this bill under discussion without looking at the historical background and the trends in the present dispute between Ottawa and the provinces. It has been suggested, unfairly, that the main difference between Quebec separatism and western alienation is that the former is rooted in cultural aspirations while the latter is predominantly based on economic considerations. This belief places undue emphasis on contemporary disputes between Ottawa and the western provinces and ignores the evolution of a unique western Canadian political identity.
It is true, however, that the debate over resources that we are participating in today has brought the economic aspects to the forefront more than at any time in our history. The oil and gas resources in question generate billions of dollars in revenue, not just to the provincial government concerned but to the municipal and federal, regional and city governments as well. This generation of resource wealth in our economy is significant at every level of government, and because of that everyone wants to grab an overly large share of the pie. Not only that, but in the case of Alberta the oil and gas industry accounts, directly or indirectly, for one half of the jobs in that province.
With stakes so high we should not be surprised to see that provincial leaders are unprepared to make concessions which might serve as a precedent for further loss of ownership and control in the resource sector. However, since the revenue is so large, Ottawa's stake truly is very, very high; but because of that it should not be perceived in terms of a little bit more revenue. At stake is not just revenue; if they believe that is all that is important, then they are making a big mistake.
An attitude of belligerence is being perceived in the west. It is an attitude which reflects the belligerence of the central government, regardless of its political orientation. It is an attitude of belligerence expressed by the centre to its parts. Is that really worth exchanging for a few points of revenue? Personally, I do not think so.
The legal issues in this debate are also of critical importance, but I do not feel that the legal issues should be the be-all and end-all. After all, we are subject to continually changing political circumstances which should not be left at the mercy of arbitrary courtroom discussion. A legally right position is not necessarily a morally right position, or a right position as it relates to equity within the relationships of the governments in this partnership. Even if we have a federal government which can legally take revenue, and even if we have court decisions coming down on the side of federal resource control, that does not necessarily make the trend right. As we discuss this issue and as we look at the legality of it, the dollar bills involved, let us not lose sight of the morality of it. Let us not lose sight of the equity as it relates to the partners of this great nation.
Provincial efforts to develop their resources have not been made any easier by the fact that the west, especially the prairies, was originally conceived as hinterland to the industrial heartland of central Canada. It is worth noting that while the British North America Act originally granted ownership of resources to the three original provinces of Canada, similar rights were not achieved in eastern Canada until long after provincial status was achieved. The reason for this is not all that flattering to federal governments of that era, either Conservative or Liberal governments. I would like to think that throughout history the party with which I sit had, in fact, been righteous always, but that is not true of any of the parties here. Alienation is not limited to the Liberal Party of Canada, the New Democratic Party or the Conservative party. Alienation is much bigger than that. It is, in fact, separate and apart from the various political entities which have controlled this country in the past and which, of course, are attempting to maintain the status quo. As my hon. friend for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) was speaking he mentioned alienation, and I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) holler across the chamber, "What does that have to do with this bill, these western concerns you are talking about? Get back to the bill."

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the asides of members opposite will be reported. They ask me to stop talking about alienation and start talking about the bill. If there is any member of this House of Commons who can separate western concerns and western alienation from this bill which we are discussing I would invite them to come to western Canada in order to express that kind of separation. Mr. Speaker, I invite you to try to make that separation. The two are so intensely
June 2, 1981

intertwined. If we could only get the message across, if all the speakers who have spoken here could get that message across and none other, then we would, in fact, be accomplishing a significant amount. Of course, the most important step which we would accomplish would be that this bill would not pass if an understanding of the situation in the west were held by members opposite.
In the interim between 1867 and 1930, when the prairie provinces were granted ownership of their resources, minerals had become an increasingly important source of revenue. At that point they were negotiable, the federal government was willing to say to the provinces, "All right, we will give you this revenue sharing. We will give you this source of revenue." Times have changed. At that time the government was a small part of our lives, now it is such a big part of our lives that the centre must acquire more revenue to waste in various massive government expenditure programs. The federal government granted provincial status to Manitoba in 1870 and to Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905, but Ottawa retained control over their natural resources until 1930. When ownership was finally transferred to the provinces, the principle of control was that set out in section 109 of the BN A Act of 1867, which reads:
All lands, mines, minerals, and royalties belonging to the several provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at the Union, and all sums then due and payable for such lands, mines, minerals, or royalties, shall belong to the several provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick in which the same are situate or arise, subject to any trusts existing in respect thereof, and to any interest other than that of the province in the same.
The intent of the British North America Act at that time was very clear, but it has become less clear through central government practice.
At the same time, the prairie provinces were extended the right to impose direct taxes within the province, a right conferred on the original provinces by section 92.2 of the BN A Act. However, the BNA Act also granted considerable powers to the federal government which were to have far-reaching implications for provincial jurisdiction.
Those far-reaching implications are being felt over a hundred years later in the bill which is before us today. They are implications and not intentions which were established at the beginning of confederation. It is those intentions which are being challenged here today in our opposition to this bill. Specifically, section 91 of the BNA Act conferred upon the Parliament of Canada the authority to regulate trade and commerce and the power to raise money by any mode or systems of taxation. I do not believe that, at the time these powers were conferred on the respective governments in 1867, they were intended to be absolute. Unfortunately, over time, they have become regarded in this way. The provincial view is that provincial Crown ownership is, in the words of Alberta's energy minister Merv Leitch, the "key to the answer to nearly all questions of jurisdiction over natural resources". In this view federal action is limited strictly and absolutely to specified circumstances of truly national dimensions or emergency.
Two early court cases, Smylie v R. (1900) and Brooks-Bid-lake v A.G. British Columbia (1923) supported this view. Both cases involved the right of provinces to place certain conditions
Excise Tax
on the sale of timber abroad. Both judgments ruled in favour of provincial jurisdiction. More recent decisions show that the passage of time has modified legal views on the question of resource ownership. The federal position today is that Section 91 of the BNA Act gives them considerable scope for acting within the realm of resource control. They agree that the two cases I referred to earlier, Smylie and Brooks-Bidlake, do not apply when there is a question of provincial property, proprietary rights, versus federal powers over trade, commerce and taxation.
Two recent Supreme Court decision, Canadian Oil and Gas v. The Government of Saskatchewan (1977) and Central Canada Potash v. The Government of Saskatchewan, seem to support the federal position. In the first case, the government of Saskatchewan expropriated all oil and gas rights in the province and set up royalty and tax structures which would have effectively allowed the government to gather for itself all excess profits resulting from the sharp rise in the price of oil. The Supreme Court ruled that this represented an indirect taxation and was hence beyond provincial control because oil price increases would be passed on to the consumer instead of being taken directly from the producer. Moreover, it was found to intrude upon federal authority over trade and commerce because 98 per cent of Saskatchewan's oil was exported at that time. The second case, Central Canada Potash, involved an attempt by the Saskatchewan government to legislate the rationing of potash production between various producers. The potential of Central Canada Potash would have been greatly reduced by this action, and it appealed to the Supreme Court, which ruled that the issue was one of external trade, and thus the responsibility of the federal government. These decisions were the latest development in a process best summarized by S. I. Bushnell:
The present trend of the interpretation of the trade and commerce power by the Supreme Court of Canada towards restriction of provincial power over matters which have economic ramifications outside the province, lead to the conclusion that control over natural resources has passed to the dominion through the trade and commerce power.
The decision in this court case is, in fact, one of the most significant in setting this trend toward federal control and ownership of resources. It is this trend, which is being established by precedent, which is so alarming to western Canada. This trend is further fortified by bills like this which set another form of precedent and another form of taking control. This affects the very basis, future, and potential of the provinces.
We have more recently seen the federal government employ the trade and commerce provision to hold down the price of domestic oil and use its tax power to capture the difference between the domestic price and the export price. Efforts by the provinces to halt this process have been countered by federal government measures, which were apparently legal, according to the strictest letter of the law, but which were hardly equitable to the producing provinces.

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
When one gets down to a debate of legality versus equitabil-ity, one finds western Canada to be in an impossible situation, because how can unequal parts ever be equal? When all the power and all the structure is based at the centre, and we are seeking equity, how can we possibly get it when we do not have the legal capacity or the power structure to make the changes? For example, when both Alberta and Saskatchewan attempted to raise royalty rates to take advantage of a massive oil increase in 1973, Ottawa responded by removing deductibility on royalty payments on federal income taxes paid by all companies. Rather than place such a heavy burden on the producers, who backed down? Was it the federal government, which should have backed down in the interest of Canada, in the interest of the region and in the interest of the producer? No, it was the provincial government which backed down in a spirit of compromise and a spirit of reality, it gave in; but by giving in, it gave everything that it had. It gave away the few levers of power that it had in a spirit of good will and in an attempt to come to some sort of compromise. Now it is left with very little.
The Lougheed government is attempting to use the only tool left to it, and that is control over production. However, this federal government and this House of Commons have allowed even that to be taken from Alberta, from the regions, and from the provinces. It has not just affected Alberta. It has affected the whole of Canada. We seem to view this so often as a set-up between a province and the country. But it is not a province versus the country; it is all for the benefit, or should be for the benefit, of the country. However, the federal government is prepared to take back this last tool through what it defines as an emergency. This Energy Supplies Emergency Act leaves very little in the hands of the provinces, and much less than was originally envisaged in the BNA Act of 1867.
In the words of Professor A. Thompson, the game is over if, in addition to setting prices unilaterally, Ottawa can compel the resource-owning provinces to sell. At that point, no real bargaining power is left to the province. De facto expropriation has occurred.
Can we move to de facto expropriation, the federal government, in fact, accomplishing expropriation of its parts? That is the question. Can we? The federal government seems willing to bargain with that, to play with that, and to take that chance of making the big grab; and it is losing all, because I do not think that the western part of this country can possibly accept that one last straw. That is what we are reaching.
It is so hard to explain that in this House of Commons. It is so hard to explain that to hon. members opposite who say we should get on with the issue of the bill when that is, in fact, the heart and soul and the very basic issue of the most important problem facing Canada today. It is that one more little step which is breaking the relationship of the parts to the centre.
Today we are discussing part of the enacting legislation of the National Energy Program which has continued this tradition of federal intrusion into provincial rights, but has again added a new precedent and a new element. Besides continuing to hold the price of oil below world levels and introducing new
tax on net revenues, the federal government, for the first time, introduced a natural gas-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am also glad to participate in the debate during the report stage of Bill C-57 which is now before the House. In view of the limited time we have on such a fundamental bill, I will try to make my remarks fairly short and concise. I guess this is always an interesting challenge for any hon. member, and it certainly is for this hon. member. I do not intend to become involved with this question of alienation of regions today.
We have heard quite a bit from hon. members, and certainly from those from the west. I think they have justification to feel very aggrieved at certain elements of this excise tax bill, which is what it is, in terms of how it affects the natural resources of a very specific part of the country, namely, western Canada. Without getting into the exchange which has taken place between hon. members from time to time, my fundamental concern with this bill is what will be done if this bill is enacted. Certainly, those in the viewing public and in the galleries must feel that this is pretty dry subject matter. It is the type of thing which does not only relate to regional alienation, but also raises the fundamental question of how the whole parliamentary process alienates the people.
The indexation of excise taxes started out on a quarterly basis, and I gather it is now based on the cost of living on a yearly basis. This really takes away the very real and historic reason as to why there is such an institution as Parliament. You, Your Honour, know well your history, and some of us know our history to a point. This whole parliamentary process started with the fundamental battle of the power of the purse. Parliament was not called together to legislate laws relating to all the social injustices of the land and to pass unemployment insurance bills and medicare bills which have evolved as society has evolved. It was a fundamental fight between the old king and his dukes and lords to try to raise the money so that the king could fight the wars of the crusades. That, in an elementary way and oversimplified to a point, is how Parliament-from the French word "pari" meaning to speak-came to oversee expenditures. I do not know about the ladies but, in effect, the lords and dukes said, "Look, Mr. King, we are going to provide the horses to fight the crusades and money to help pay the soldiers, so we want to have something to say about when we fight and who we fight, or if we fight all the time and whether we are going to have another War of the Roses for 100 years." It is the basic principle, the power of the purse from which the parliamentary system evolved and accordingly, it is how society evolved. At least once a year Parliament had a budget and the elected representatives of the people could decide what would be done with the money.
Some people might suggest that we may be getting into that kind of imperial trapping here with the long-time government
June 2, 1981

by one party. In effect, the people were able to tell the rulers or the prime minister of the day that they did not like a particular tax and that they would not vote for it.
Once the principle of indexation of the excise tax is established, Mr. Speaker, why would the government stop there? Why not have an indexation of income tax and corporation tax? In many countries, as in this, the parliamentary process has fallen into disrepute and it is under attack because of the social order of the day. We all know that of the 150 countries that constitute the United Nations, only about 25 have the type of government that we have.
As the intention of this bill is to index taxes, it is not beyond the realm of argument that the next thing would be to index income taxes and then corporation taxes. In that case, why need Parliament meet? Everything could be tied to a computer and to the cost of living. All we would have to do is push a button at home. That is what I find iniquitous and why I reject this bill.
Traditionally, ministers of finance have had to come into this chamber and face the people who are sent here to talk about finances and the taxes of the day.
The problem is not just the alienation of region against region which appears in this bill, but there is also the potential for a further alienation of the public from the whole parliamentary process.
There is a specific example of this which affects everyone who imbibes at all. It is something about which the working man, about whom we properly hear so much, should be aware and concerned, and that is the effect of indexation of the excise tax on the price of beer. Other members have spoken of how the iniquitous increases are beginning to challenge the way the Canadian consumer spends his leisure time if he wants to have some liquid refreshment. I do not think any country has ever tried to influence social mores by means of a tax bill and I do not think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) wants to do this either, but such is the direct effect of the excise tax.
It will mean a 29 per cent increase in the price of beer, a 155 per cent increase in the price of wine, but only a 6 per cent increase in the price of distilled spirits. When this indexation is compounded to 1991, it is clear that the cost of a two-dozen case of small bottles of beer will have increased by 157 per cent and will cost the consumer $23.64. By the same indexing principle, compounded to 1991, a 25-ounce bottle of relatively inexpensive gin will have increased 101 per cent but will only cost $16.42.
It does not take a teetotaler to appreciate the effect this will have on our social mores. We have to recognize that there are those who like to imbibe. Rightly or wrongly, the libation at five o'clock or six o'clock has become a way of life in most western industrialized countries-even in Russia I am told they imbibe the odd vodka. I do not know if they have beer in Russia, but if they do, I am sure that the working man who goes to his commune and votes for his commissars would not put up with a massive increase in the price to the tune of
Excise Tax
$23.64 for a two dozen case, compared to someone paying $16.42 for his gin or vodka. Revolutions have started on less provocation than the sledge-hammer approach of this excise tax index, compounded to produce this result.
While this appears to be a dry debate, there are elements which have some very real liquid connotations. As long as we talk only about the libation liquid and not about blood in the streets from the revolution which my hon. friend for Halifax-West (Mr. Crosby) mentioned, we need not worry, but all the same, revolutions have been started for less.
I say very seriously that this bill is bad in principle. It means more than the alienation of the region which is involved in the wellhead tax and the production tax on the natural resources of the west when there is no such tax on the natural resources of other parts of the country such as nickel, copper or electricity. The attitude is to grab some money-take it from the well. There will surely be alienation of the people who will be hit by this excise tax compounded and indexed to the cost of living. The government, which is not supposed to profit from inflation, has tried, as we all know, to index away the effects of inflation on personal income tax. But through this bill, if the cost of living goes up, so does the excise tax and the revenue to the government.
For that reason alone, I would have no hesitation in voting against this bill and I am glad to have the opportunity to speak against it this afternoon because of the effect it will have on the parliamentary process.
I see it is just about six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so before I go on with my other points, may I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the order of the House earlier, I know we have limited time and there are not many minutes left. Without reviewing what I said before the supper break, I do want to say that Bill C-57 is a pretty dry sounding bill. It deals with excise tax and what it will do to Canadians from coast to coast, be they high income or low income Canadians, be they people who like spirits or wine or people who like beer. This bill packs a hefty wallop. Revolutions have been caused by incidents less iniquitous than those contained in this bill. Canadian people who, in the heat of the summer, might like their draught of beer are going to be rather

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
concerned with the indexing provided by this bill. The minister may laugh, he may like the odd beer too, I do not know about that. But Canadians from coast to coast will realize that for the first time we are putting an indexing clause in a tax bill, not to help the aggrieved taxpayer to pay his taxes, but rather a clause whereby taxes will rise if the cost of living increases. This will occur to such an extent that a case of two dozen beer in small bottles, not the great big quarts that people in Atlantic Canada used to know in the days of yore, will increase by 157 per cent by 1991. Therefore, in 1991 a case of two dozen beer will cost $23.64. On the other hand, there will be an increase of 101 per cent on a bottle of gin, whoever drinks that, or vodka and some of the other imported liquor under indexation and the compounding of it, which is adding tax to tax. However, a 25-ounce bottle of gin or vodka will cost $16.42.
This is an iniquitous tax. If this Parliament approves a bill that forever and a day establishes a precedent for future days, not in the days of yore, then all taxes might as well be calculated according to the cost of living index. Why not calculate the personal income tax according to the cost of living index? Why not calculate corporation tax or for that matter any other type of tax in that way?
I say to hon. members that this is a fundamental affront to the whole reason why this place first began many years ago when the old dukes and the lords sat together and addressed the king. 1 am not referring to Mackenzie King but to the old royal kings. It might have been Mackenzie King, too, but in the old days they said "Look, Mr. King, you cannot fight the wars of the crusades unless we have a say in what you are going to do." That is why Parliament started under the old English system. It was the power of the purse, and who was going to impose taxes. Did the people have the right to send representatives to the capital of the land to discuss taxes?
But when there is an excise tax which affects items in this country, let alone beer which some people like to enjoy, I say it is an iniquitous bill. For that reason alone, I am very happy to speak against it in a constructive way.
I said earlier that we are not talking about the alienation of regions. We all know now that people think different things about members of Parliament, about what members can do and what they cannot do. Many people think that members of Parliament are trying to do things to them through the back pocket or via the open door.
I believe in this place. These are the words of the late right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert whose shadow still falls from time to time on this House, to its betterment. This is the only institution that is the embodiment of the personification of 22 million or 24 million Canadians, however many there may be tomorrow, on June 3, when we are all supposed to sign our census forms. Parliament is the living organ from coast to coast.
I could speak a long time about this. While men opposite, those in government, political adversaries, respected colleagues
take a position, and I respect a person who does, I am sad about one thing. I am afraid that government ministers, not those on the back bench, have really lost touch with old Joe Canadian, old Jane Canada, Ms. Canadian, Mrs. Canadian and Mr. Canadian. They have been in power too long. They really have lost touch.
Getting off the subject of beer, which does not make this bill dry but makes it rather interesting, let us come to those things that other members have talked about in a serious vein. My whip tells me that I only have about two minutes left. I will not repeat all that was said about the inequities of the production tax, the 8 per cent wellhead tax, taxation of the natural resources in the west when we do not tax other natural resources such as nickel, copper or electricity in other parts of the country.
After we adjourned, the six o'clock news had confirmation that this national energy policy, which should be called nationalization of energy productivity, has failed. What are we facing here tonight? As was the case in the Constitution debate, again the government is impervious to the comments of hon. members who have a larger view of the power and the potential of Canada than the narrow, centralist concept espoused, most notably by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his chief energy aid, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). I returned this morning from a conference of educators in Winnipeg. We were discussing some of the larger questions of development and Canada's role therein. Some of those educators from across Canada turned their attention to the inability of Canada to make clear, comprehensive policies in the development field when we are at such an impasse in our federal-provincial relations. The people who were there this morning are intelligent, and they were asking why we have this continued impasse in federal-provincial relations in this country. It is madness, so much so that one person even suggested that if somebody could figure out a way to solve the federal-provincial deadlock and stop the wars which are going on in this country, that person would deserve the Nobel peace prize.
What we have now is a second imposition of a cutback in production by the province of Alberta. Alberta has now cut back production by 120,000 barrels a day in an effort to make clear to the federal government that a fair and just energy policy and pricing scheme and formula must be arrived at in the interests of all Canadians. We have had imposed on us a levy at the pump to pay for the resulting increased importation of oil.
We already know we are paying $5.5 billion a year- perhaps it will go up to $6 billion before this year is out-for imported oil while oil is lying in the ground in Canada which could be used instead. We have been through this many times in the House of Commons. I will not delay the debate any more tonight except to ask, on behalf of the people who sent me here and on behalf of Canadians as a whole, when this impasse will come to an end. When will we stop seeing oil rigs being driven out of the oil-producing provinces? Up to now, 139 oil rigs have been driven out of the country; 63 more are to follow. Tonight I want to deal with one very small segment of this bill, that is motion No. 9 in the name of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and I thank him for putting it on the Order Paper. He and I had some discussions on this, and while I could not possibly attend the various meetings in committee-and I make no bones about the fact that I do not get very involved in tax bills-they bother me more than just a little bit. Nonetheless, this particular item is one in which I am particularly interested. It has to do with the removal of the provision for commercial air service operators to deduct the tax on aviation gasoline used in flight training. This is an example, Mr. Speaker, of the government, as it has done in the past, taking a pot-shot at a very small segment of the economy, one with very little ability to fight back because it is not as big as the airlines, the banks or many other segments of the economy. In fact, it is made up of some very fine people who are very concerned about that segment of the economy.
The commercial air service operators who provide flight training are very concerned that the importance of this training is being lost sight of, as evidenced by these tax measures. In the mini-budget of April 21 last year, the sales tax exemption for commercial aircraft was amended to exclude aircraft used in flight training. In the same budget it was confirmed that refunds of the excise tax on aviation gasoline, which was imposed in December, 1978 ostensibly for non-commercial users, would not be available for flight training activity.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to take a moment and put on the record a picture of one of these small fixed-base operators. The one I will use as an example is a man named Jim Marker. Jim Marker has been involved in the education of students of flying in the Belleville area. In fact, he has been involved in all sorts of flying in the Belleville area for these many years. He is a very dedicated man. I doubt very much if he has ever taken a cent out of the business which he has supported so loyally for these past two decades. As a matter of fact, I know he has put money into the business on a regular basis. In fact, his position

as a vice-president of a major corporation in the Belleville area is all that allows him to do this job as well as he does.
There was a need for better facilities for flying in the Belleville area a couple of decades ago. At that time there were no government measures which would allow for the development of this sort of industry in a small community like Belleville. Jim Marker bought the land, and having bought it he cleared it, cut down the trees and made it ready. He erected a small building on it to act as an office and a centre for pilots. It contained a room in which pilots would receive their ground schooling. In the very early days, of course, in the spring, it was all mud, so Jim went out and bought gravel with money out of his own pocket and spread that gravel on the runway to keep the mud down.
Obviously, any activity of this sort requires aircraft. So Jim went out and bought the aircraft, again out of his own pocket. In order to repair the aircraft he trained himself to be a first class mechanical engineer capable and licensed by the Department of Transport to repair aircraft. When it was obvious in the wintertime that the cost of having the snow removed from the runway to allow flights in the wintertime would be too expensive, Jim went out and bought a secondhand grader. He keeps the grader in excellent shape in order to keep the runway clear through all types of weather, all winter long.
In the summertime, of course, grass grows up over the runway, for it is a grass airstrip. While I had an opportunity in the few years when I was mayor of the city of Belleville to quietly help him by lending him some parks equipment every once in a while, to keep the grass under control, that has not been the case since. So Jim went out and bought a tractor to cut his own grass. He rides around in the evening and on Saturdays to cut the grass, since it is necessary to keep it done. He has built more hangars. In fact, he has been the strongest supporter of general aviation in the area that this country has ever seen. He stands out as a monument, as one who has devoted a good part of his life to general aviation. Now, Mr. Speaker, Jim will be taxed again. He has one voice in this House of Commons, and I am proud to be that voice. I hope that members of the House will understand that I am speaking on behalf of all the Jim Markers all across Canada who are oppressed by this particular tax.
The commercial flying training segment of the Canadian air transport industry has, over the years, served Canada very well, not only in times of national emergency but through its continued support in the development of the vital Canadian air transport system. This segment of the industry formed the nucleus for the British Air Commonwealth training program, a major contribution throughout all of the Second World War.
The benefits of a vigorous air transport industry to the development of Canada and its economic and cultural growth have been well recognized. The survival and the continued growth of this dynamic industry is dependent upon the preservation of a healthy, well-equipped and professional pilot training service. It is essential that Canada maintain an adequate
Excise Tax
pool of well-trained and experienced pilots to meet the present and future requirements for all classes of commercial air services, as well as government air services, corporate operations, military support and any future national emergencies. I know that one of the young men who trained in the Belleville area now flies for Air Canada. I should not really say only one, Mr. Speaker, since I know that there are more than one, there are a few. Some have gone to the military. The interest in flying training is something that, when engendered in a young man, usually turns out for the best of the country. Without that vital support, the Canadian air transport industry would be unable to accommodate the requirements of the public for essential air services from Canadian resources.
It is obvious that up to date professional training organizations play an important role in achieving and maintaining an acceptable level of Canadian flight safety, not only within the air transport industry but throughout the private and corporate sectors as well. Acquisition of modern, well-equipped aircraft is essential in order to train pilots to operate safely and efficiently in today's complicated environment. Flying training facilities and operations traditionally receive an exceptionally low potential return on investment, particularly as potential pilot entry into commercial aviation must, of necessity, be within an age group which is not able to afford high cost training.
As I said a moment ago, Jim Marker has probably not taken a red cent out of his operation in Belleville, yet it is open to people who fly across Canada. We have pilots who drop in to Jim Marker's facilities; the guest book is filled with people's names, from east, west, south and north. They land and use the facilities at no cost. There is no $5 landing fee in Belleville.
It must be recognized that virtually all flying training schools, such as the one about which I have been speaking, and clubs, are also licensed to conduct other commercial air services, some of which are exempt from the sales tax and gasoline excise tax. Mr. Marker has a small charter operation and runs some sightseeing flights. He maintains personnel at his facilities year round to service aircraft. He also maintains pilots and instructors who are on duty all the time. With relatively small fleets of aircraft, it is not possible to dedicate an aircraft to any one class for which the operator is licensed, but the aircraft must be utilized in all phases of the operation. The same aircraft Jim uses to take someone up to do aerial photography is the one that I may well use, if I happen to be in Belleville. Just recently I took the mayor, the city manager and some other very important people from the Moira River Conservation Authority for a flight up and down the Moira River. At that time the river was in flood and some 500 or 600 acres of the city were under water and many thousands of acres outside the city. The same aircraft I used for that trip will be used for flying training one day and for a charter flight the next.
It is also important, of course, to learn appropriate lessons from past experience. In 1977, in the national interest, the Department of Manpower and Immigration deemed it necessary to restrict the issuance of Canadian work permits to

He knows that the radio facilities which are there are provided free of charge. There is no input from the federal government. Here we are, adding another tax on top of all of those taxes that the ordinary user of aircraft gasoline is faced with. The figure last fall was around 13 cents a litre, and now it is closer to 17 cents a litre. That is just in taxes and fees charged by the various levels of government against the private aircraft user, and particularly those who are using it for flying training.
It is coming at us from all sides. At another time and in another place, I intend to spend some time talking about the effect of the move by the Department of Revenue to reduce the income tax exemption for flying training to 35 hours. That is another very unsafe way of collecting a very few pennies. However, those few pennies are very important to those of us who are involved in flying training. They are very important to a segment of the economy in which people have dedicated a tremendous part of their lives to this very important activity. I want to say, as strongly as I possibly can, that this motion No. 9, in the name of the hon. member for Edmonton West is one that I want to support as strongly as I possibly can.
