speechtext:
I thank Your Honour for the opportunity to make some remarks on Bill C-57 which is now before the House, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. At the outset, I would say that it is not my intention to direct my remarks to all the provisions of this bill
of which there are 133, but rather I want to look at some of the background of these specific provisions which we now have before us and consider them in the light of the policies from whence they come.
It is simplistic to say that the provisions for the implementation of the government's tax measures are contained in this bill. In order to understand them and appreciate the basis for those provisions, we must look at what the government intends in terms of its revenue gathering and its aims and goals for the people of Canada which it exercises through its taxation policy. Just this weekend in the maritimes we have seen evidence of the conflicting views which exist in Canada with respect to the goals for the nation, and for the goals of the private sector versus those of the public sector, and how those goals intermesh.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), in a speech before the Council of Maritime Premiers in Fredericton, New Brunswick, just this past day, said that the federal government can no longer take responsibility for redistributing wealth in Canada and that it has lost control of the resources and the financial capability of Canada to the extent that it can no longer take on this responsibility. Premier Lougheed of Alberta, speaking in Halifax just the day before, indicated in his speech that he welcomes that. He welcomes it for a very good reason, because through Canada, in the private sector and among the provinces, there is the ability to accomplish many of the goals through the exercise of the abilities and capabilities of the private sector.
Therefore, the Prime Minister, in suggesting to Canadians that his federal government can no longer take responsibility for redistributing the wealth of Canada may, in the end result, be appealing to a sense of entrepreneurship which has not been exercised here in Canada heretofore. The province of Alberta, through the private sector in Alberta, and acting through the government of Alberta, may be willing to take up that challenge and achieve these goals in that particular area. This challenge would not only be for that particular area, but for all Canadians. So we must realize that behind the taxation measures which we see before us is the real government policy, the real strength of this nation in terms of what we are able to accomplish through policies and through government and the different trends which have now become evident.
As I have already indicated, on the one part the Premier of Alberta is taking the attitude and the position that the private sector can accomplish much, while on the other, the Prime Minister of Canada is saying that unless drastic measures are taken the government can no longer take responsibility for redistributing wealth in Canada. We have to ask, who ever asked the Prime Minister of Canada to take that kind of responsibility? Certainly we want and require a level of services which is standardized throughout Canada so that all Canadians will receive services. However, to go beyond that and to talk about the authority and the power to redistribute wealth is an entirely different proposition. Therefore, when the Prime Minister of Canada stands before the Council of Maritime Premiers and before Canadians and says that he no
June 2, 1981

longer has the ability to redistribute wealth in Canada, many people welcome that remark and say that it never was his authority, and that it never was his responsibility to take on that challenge.
I want to relate some of those general remarks to the provisions in this bill because what we are looking at is an attempt to regain that ability to redistribute wealth and to regain the power and authority to gather in all the funds, the money which gives authority to that power. In the world we live in we have to recognize that money is power, that those who control the purse strings and those who have the financial resources can exercise control well beyond the simplistic dollars which are involved, because, as I have said, money is power in so many ways. So we have to look at these provisions in that light. Is this really an attempt to gain power? What is the government trying to do through the exercise of its legislative authority through this House of Commons under Bill C-57?
I say to Your Honour and to other people in this House that it is merely an implementation of a government policy to gain the financial capability which it perceives it has lost. Therefore, in spite of the Prime Minister's words, he does want, and he wants on behalf of his government and his party, to regain the ability to redistribute wealth in Canada and, in that way, control not only the private sector and that which is rightfully in the public sector, but control the whole economy. We have to look at the provisions of Bill C-57 in that light.
In that connection, I want to refer to the change which is evident in federal-provincial financial arrangements which have already been announced by the Government of Canada and by the Prime Minister, and have been evidenced by his establishment, through this House of Commons, of the task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. Again we see this shift and concern on the part of the Government of Canada for its eroding position in relation to its revenue-gathering abilities, and as it relates those revenue-gathering abilities to its capacity to control the economy and the people of Canada.
What we have through this federal-provincial task force is a vehicle to spread the message of the Government of Canada, which we hear time and time again in this House in other ways and which we see evidenced here in this Bill C-57; that is, that the government needs more money. That is its problem. It is not getting its money.
I will explain why the Government of Canada is not getting the money that it needs to exercise the kind of financial and economic control that it has in the past. The reason is very simple. It is that the wealth of this country has shifted from the manufacturing sector, from the pure business community, to the natural resource community; that is to say, the wealth of this country is now evidenced by its natural resources and its ability to deal with those natural resources. The funds from them are now very clearly flowing to the provinces and the people who control the natural resources; they are not going through the same process as they have gone through in the past. In particular, that means that those who control the
Excise Tax
manufacturing and secondary industries in this country no longer have the financial clout and power that they had in the past. The government has to adjust to this change.
What the government is really doing is shifting taxation to that resource area in a way that has not been done in the past. What is at stake is not any great policy; it is just the gathering of dollar bills and the philosophy that with those dollar bills the future of this country can be controlled. We must examine the provisions of Bill C-57 in that light and ask what the end product will be, and why the government is moving in this direction.
Even though I come from eastern Canada, a part of the country that does not share the resource revenues at the present time, I have sympathy for the western provinces and for the philosophy espoused by Premier Lougheed in Halifax, Nova Scotia, the other night.
What the premier is objecting to is this reaction by the Government of Canada to the shift in power. The government is not willing to let the economy take its course, and transmit wealth. It is holding on to what it perceives as belonging to it in a way that works to the detriment of those people in the private sector and the resource-producing provinces which now have control of this wealth. It is not a simple matter of legislating a tax by means of this bill; it is a matter of legislating, assisting and conniving the transfer of power that the government seeks through this bill.
What I am referring to, Mr. Speaker, is the 8 per cent tax on petroleum and natural gas that will be imposed when this bill is passed. I realize and recognize, as do many Canadians, that to a great extent this will benefit many people in Canada. But we have to ask ourselves whether the fact that it is beneficial to a great many people is justification for the action. It is a question to which I am prepared to answer that I do not think it is the proper way to do it-to legislate through this Parliament the transfer of authority from the provincial authority that has these resources, to the federal authority that wants to hold on to its ability to redistribute wealth in Canada.
There are other methods to accomplish the same end but they involve agreement, reconciliation and understanding between the regions of the country. The ultimate result of enforced policy is rejection of that policy. That is what will happen if Parliament insists on this transfer of wealth through a legislative provision which implements a government policy of requiring that wealth produced by the resources of western Canada, and in particular Alberta and Saskatchewan, being transferred back to the central authority by means of an act of Parliament.
I do not believe that will work, Mr. Speaker. I believe that the government is making a serious mistake in taking that approach to the problem. It is avoiding the real issue, which is that there is a rationalization through which we can reach a mutual agreement for a sensible pricing formula for oil and gas. I realize that it may not be the price that the premier of Alberta would like and it may not be the price that we in

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
eastern Canada are willing to pay at this point because we want the lowest acceptable price that can be enforced on the people of western Canada, and the governments concerned, for their oil and gas.
I think this bill avoids the real issue, Mr. Speaker. The government may think that it is solving its immediate problem by gathering revenue through this source, but an enlarged problem faces us in the years ahead. That problem can only be resolved if agreement is reached on what is a fair and equitable distribution of the resources and the proceeds of the sale of the oil and gas owned by the western provinces.
I am not one of those who says that we should go through with this because we in the east will benefit from it and it will remove our immediate problem. I think the problem has to be attacked on a broader base. The government is shying away from its responsibility in this area and it is just simplistic to blame the governments of Alberta and, to a certain extent, Saskatchewan, for the failure to reach agreement on an appropriate price for oil and gas and to substitute this taxation measure for that agreement.
I think that members on this side of the House are right when they object to Parliament being a party to the enforcement of this government policy. The government, concerned with its eroding position with respect to revenues, is simply using this taxation policy as a means of transferring resources.
In the case of the east coast, that area of Canada which borders on the Atlantic Ocean and which claims submarine lands that lie under it, the government is not even giving it the benefit of a statutory implementation of its policy; it is simply attempting to seize those resources, whereas it is depriving the western provinces through a taxation policy. The government will not face up to the claim of the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland to these resources. It simply denies their claim and uses its powers and capacity as the central authority to seize them.
This is more than a shame for the Government of Canada, Mr. Speaker; it is a shame for all members of Parliament opposite who participate in it. They are denying to the people of the Atlantic coast, particularly in the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, the possibility of going beyond their dependence on federal transfer payments and federal welfare payments and moving into a new era where the resources can be developed for the benefit of the people.
We can see how the central government contributes to this strife and difficulty which sets region against region. I hope we on the east coast will not be drawn into the centralist view of coming down on those western provinces which have, by their own fortuitous circumstances, achieved a measure of wealth. I hope that we will not support the federal government in this war on western Canada and the seizure of its assets on the basis that the federal government will distribute those assets across Canada, perhaps to the momentary benefit of eastern Canada.
It is evident from the policy of the government on Bill C-48, the Canada Oil and Gas Act, that it plans the same kind of
future for Newfoundland and Nova Scotia if those provinces are able to achieve the level of resource richness enjoyed in western Canada.
Whether hon. members opposite recognize it or not, the central government is setting itself not only against the western area of the country but against the east coast as well. It will not be very long before the province of Newfoundland and the province of Alberta are joined in battle. The battle they will be joining is the implementation of the policy now before us. Through its legal capabilities, its lawyers, its counsel, its many consultants, the federal government knows a great many techniques by which to accomplish its end. Unfortunately, the new techniques which the government uses to accomplish its ends are not acceptable to the people of Canada. The technique of establishing a taxation policy to accomplish ends that were not intended to be within the power and authority of the Government of Canada are not acceptable. But that is what is happening via this bill. The government is using its taxation policy to accomplish its end, and its end is the control of wealth in Canada. That would be acceptable only if the control of wealth was for the purpose of establishing and supporting federal programs required by all Canadians. But that is not the end purpose of the Government of Canada. Its purpose is to go further and control all Canadians and to gain control for the purpose of perpetuating itself in office, and for no higher purpose than that.
Let me turn to some of the specific provisions in the bill beyond that provision to which I have already referred, and that is the taxation on natural resources, in other words, our oil and gas. There are other areas in which the government has tried to enforce its policy. I am thinking of the taxation of beer and wine which again is unacceptable to a great many people. We ought to foster, through government policy, moderation in the use of spirits. We ought to ensure that taxation permits moderation and encourages people to utilize beer and wine, the more moderate spirits, over the alcoholic liquors. There are many other things I could mention but as my time is coming to an end, I want to conclude by saying that there are serious objections to this bill. We will have to take them into consideration when we vote.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in the debate on Bill C-57. Essentially I want to talk about the impact this bill will have on the artists of Canada.
Various speeches have been made in this House outlining some of our objections to this bill. I understand even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has talked about the inequities and evil of taxing spirits covered by this bill. In any event, I leave that topic to other members.
I wish to speak on the imposition of the sales tax on prints and original works of art, of which there are limited editions and copies. I shall talk about the government's stupidity in imposing a sales tax on these works of art. This is a provision about which the whole artistic community is scratching its
June 2, 1981

head. In fact, the artistic community is downright angry at the blatant lack of wisdom in the imposition of such a tax under Bill C-57. What the bill essentially fails to do is to distinguish between original prints and reproductions manufactured by mechanical means. It is the inability of people in the Department of Finance to see that difference and to express that difference in law.
What the proposal will do is to reclassify artists and master printers as manufacturers. This is something which the visual artists in this country are not quite willing to accept. The effect of Bill C-57 will make works of art more expensive. It will make it more difficult for artists to sell their work to the private sector and to galleries. The income of over 50 per cent of full-time artists is roughly $6,000 a year or less, and making their work more expensive will make it more difficult for them to sell it. A fair number of individual artists supplement their income by having a run of sometimes 30, 40 or, at the most, 100 prints. These are wood block prints, stone prints and various other kinds of prints. These prints are generally sold through galleries. They provide an important subsidy to many visual artists. The sale of prints is also very important to a fair number of galleries. The selling of prints is generally the bread and butter for a lot of small private commercial galleries. This tax imposes an extra burden. It also adds an extra burden on the publishing and printing industry, that small section of our publishing industry which prints original fine art graphics. This tax is a needless hindrance. As well, it has some interesting implications with regard to the general acceptance of the free flow of art through international boundaries. Through this bill we will create a blockage, if you can call it such, of works of art coming in from other countries.
Most of the Inuit and native people's art consists of variations of prints. Again, an extra tax is being imposed on this art form. It is a stupid piece of legislation because it will cost more to collect the tax than the amounts of money which will accrue to the government. It is a blind interference in the art community. Furthermore, this tax will be difficult to apply. It will be a bureaucratic nightmare.
Through this bill, the government is discriminating against a particular form of art. Prints are one form of art. There are other forms of art, for instance, oils, acrylics and so on. What this tax does is to make one particular type of art form more expensive because of the extra sales tax being imposed on print making.
The artistic community has long felt that the government does not have a coherent artistic and cultural policy for Canada. The artistic community has long complained that the actions of one ministry work against the interests and the programs of another ministry. Tonight we have a typical example of how the actions and the thinking of a group of bureaucrats in the tax department are totally at odds with the stated intention of the government in the area of cultural policy.
Right now we have the Applebaum committee which is travelling across the nation trying to put together a coherent government policy on culture. Members of this committee are
Excise Tax
listening to representations and receiving briefs from right across Canada. Yet the government does not wait for those recommendations and findings to come in. The government is acting on its own in this area. It is an area which will certainly not win the government any points in the artistic community. Instead, the government will make it more difficult for artists to survive in Canada and it will force some artists to leave Canada and attempt to sell their prints in the United States. This bill will not help the young collector, for example, the young professional person who wishes to start a small modest art collection. These are the people who generally start their collections by buying a few prints. Now the cost of prints will be even higher.
In the well thought out document entitled "A Strategy for Culture" put together by The Canadian Conference of the Arts, the authors urged that there should be tax incentives for private investors. Yet the opposite is to be found in Bill C-57 which is before us tonight. The authors of this document urge that taxation policies should be used in a systematic way as a vehicle to encourage cultural development. But we have the exact opposite in this bill tonight. The writers also urge that the visual artists and craftsmen should, in all cases, be exempt from paying sales tax on materials and production equipment and from charging sales tax on their finished work. What we have tonight is the very opposite. We have a government which has set up commissions and which states certain goals, but in its action does exactly the opposite. This is not only true in the cultural field. We have seen examples of this in many other fields. There is always the promise, always the good talk. In fact, someone called it the sweet talk from the Liberals. However the reality is to be found in what the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) says and does.
The government has indicated that it wants to develop a coherent cultural policy. However, the history of this government in the area of culture is a dismal one. Most of the major artistic institutions in this country are on the verge of bankruptcy, yet there is no immediate action from this government. All we get is another royal commission. We have artists leaving the country because they cannot make a living in Canada selling their works of art. Instead of offering assistance, the government makes it even more difficult for artists to survive in this country.
In one of their major recommendations, the Canadian Conference of the Arts recommended that the Department of Communications have some muscle, that it have some influence in what other departments do and what their policies are in terms of the arts. Bill C-57 in front of us clearly indicates that the minister in charge of cultural affairs in Canada has very little power in cabinet, even when it comes to such a minor matter, and it surely is minor to the government, as sales tax on prints.
I again return to the question of why the government is doing this. Is there any rationale? Surely fundamental wisdom would suggest that it is more of a hassle imposing this tax than

June 2, 1981
Excise Tax
it will be a benefit. The amount of money collected under this tax will be negligible. The cost of enforcing it will surely be more than what will be collected under the tax. What gives? Where is the rationale? There is no rationale.
I suggest this is just a blind bureaucracy grinding along, having its own impetus, its own power to drive it forward. Rational arguments cannot stop it. It is honest to suggest that what we find in this bill is not rationality but irrationality. It will not benefit anybody. It will hinder the growth and development of Canadian artists in this country.
In conclusion, this provision in Bill C-57 is not one that will earn the government many high points in the artistic community of this country. They will view this as another example of a blind bureaucracy grinding away with a total lack of commitment and will to make certain that we have a coherent cultural policy. Even on such a small matter they cannot be swayed from their determined path. It is an indication to the artistic community that we have a government which, despite all its brave words about Canadian culture, is not willing to take some positive steps in that direction but in fact is so ignorant that it imposes further hardships on artists in Canada today.
For that reason, and for the many other reasons my colleagues have mentioned during this debate, we will not be able to support the bill in front of us this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I would have a good lead-in if I followed the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). I now find I have an equally good lead-in following the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). He talked about confusion. I have never seen a more confused bill in my life. It is from beginning to end a mass of confused notions bringing together such disparate elements as indexation of a variety of products such as beer, tobacco and wine on the one hand, and on the other petroleum, aviation, aviation fuel, flying training, prints and books. To cap it all, there is a shift from the imperial to the metric system in measuring some of the matters on which there will be levies.
We probably have to put it down to the fact that this bill is no more than a desperate search for funds required to live up to commitments which had better not been made at all. It is a frantic look for funds. In order to deal with the unusual purchase of Petrofina, which produced not one additional drop of petroleum in this country at a cost of $1.5 billion, there is to be a levy on all home owners for heating and all car owners for driving.
Instead of investing in Canada, this government seems determined to invest in Belgium, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, and Mexico when the billions that are going overseas might be better spent here. In order to make up for that loss, there has been a scrambling around with this bill. I have forgotten how many pages there are. I am working at pages 75 and 76 because I think that is the convenient place to work.

The bill has 116 pages. It is a desperate effort to find more funds. I mention that one of the peculiarities of this bill is that in one set of clauses they deal with the levy on absolute alcohol content. There is to be a levy there of 54 cents per gallon on absolute alcohol content. I am not quite sure I know what absolute alcohol content is, but I stress the point that the tax is to be levied at so many cents per gallon. That is on page 75. In the next section we see that there is a levy of 27 cents per gallon on absolute alcohol, and in the third one, five cents per gallon on beer or malt. In the next part dealing with tobacco, cigars and cigarettes, it is so much per pound or per thousand. Going to the bottom of page 76, we find they talk about absolute ethyl alcohol. The ethyl is obviously metric. Here we have so many dollars per hectolitre.
I defy anybody on the opposite side of the House to make a comparison and tell me how much $11.88 per hectolitre is in dollars per gallon. Is there anyone opposite who can do so? I bet the Metric Commission cannot do it. How about it? How many dollars per gallon is $11.88 per hectolitre? Work it out. While they are working it out, I will go to the next one.
They are still trying to figure that out over there. You can talk about confusion, but why should one type of absolute alcohol have a levy placed on it per gallon, and poor old ethyl be subject to a metric level?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: What about Mabel?

speechtext:
They have not got to "mabel" syrup at all. In any event, this is just one of the idiocies or confusions brought about by this particular bill.
Have you got it worked out yet? Apparently he has not.
On the serious side, and that is serious enough, we have to wonder whether the government should really be using tax incentives or disincentives to change the drinking patterns of the people of this country. You know what this government has done? We have a breakdown of the statistics on the changes in drinking habits of the people of this country from 1974 to 1980. There has been a drop in the consumption of beer as a result of levies placed on it, I think per gallon, but I am not sure, of 3.6 per cent over a matter of nine months, and a drop in wine consumption, but an increase of 4.6 per cent in the consumption of distilled spirits. This may very well be because of the distinction between gallons and litres, a litre being smaller with more of it being bought, but in any event there was an increase in the consumption of distilled liquor. I think that is a very dangerous trend. I am sure all our police forces in this country would deplore this emphasis on hard liquor, as certainly the beer industry does.
I wonder, however, whether it is the distilling industry which has this particular government by the left hand, that is urging it to increase the levy on beer while decreasing the levy percentagewise on distilled spirits in order that it can contribute more to that Liberal party.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), since he cannot calculate the dif-
June 2, 1981

ference between gallons and hectolitres, to the economic effect of this shift in consumption from high to low alcoholic content beverages on the agricultural industry. The economic impact on the brewing industry and on the agricultural producers, who depend on the brewing industry, will be severe. That is pointed out in a letter I have from the Brewers Association of Canada. Some 63 per cent of the value of agricultural products destined for use in producing all domestically consumed alcoholic beverages is purchased by the brewing industry, and it is being taxed more heavily. If beer sales continue to decline, the brewing industry agricultural purchases, which amounted to almost $100 million in 1979, will decline accordingly. According to the figures which are produced here, that decline will turn out to be something of the order of 8 per cent or 9 per cent.
1 should like to go on and quote further from this particular letter. I admit that it is biased in favour of the brewing industry and against the distilling industry, but the indexation notion is criticized severely.
I see the Speaker is becoming a little anxious. I reserve my right to come back to this when the matter comes forward again under other amendments.
